title: Linux & the Command Line
why: Nearly every server, container, and cloud VM you'll ever touch runs Linux, not Windows or macOS -- and you control all of them the same way: through a text shell, not a mouse. This module builds real command-line fluency (navigation, file operations, permissions, processes, package management, and basic scripting) that every later module -- Docker, CI/CD, Kubernetes, cloud providers -- assumes you already have.

topics.title: Why Linux runs the cloud
topics.concept: Almost every public cloud VM image, every Docker container base image, and nearly all production servers run some Linux distribution -- not Windows, not macOS. This isn't tradition: Linux is free and open-source (no per-server licensing cost at cloud scale), it's scriptable and automatable down to the kernel, and its process/permission model was designed from the start for many users and services sharing one machine safely. A SHELL is the program that reads text commands you type and runs them -- the interface you'll use for everything in this module. On Windows, you can get a real Linux shell either via WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux, a genuine Ubuntu install running alongside Windows) or Git Bash (a lighter, POSIX-compatible shell bundled with Git for Windows, which is what runs the examples in this module).
topics.analogy: Choosing Linux for servers is like a shipping company choosing standardized steel containers over hand-built wooden crates: the format is open, free to use, identical everywhere, and built specifically for handling at scale -- not because it's fancier, but because uniformity and low cost compound massively once you have thousands of them.

examples.code:
echo "hello from the shell"
whoami
pwd
examples.note: echo prints text back to you, whoami prints your logged-in username, and pwd ("print working directory") shows where you currently are in the filesystem. These three commands are your proof-of-life check in any new shell -- if they run, your shell works.

mistakes: Typing shell commands into a text editor, browser address bar, or chat window instead of an actual terminal -- nothing happens because nothing is running them.
Assuming a cloud VM will default to Windows -- most cloud provider default images, and virtually all official Docker base images (node, python, postgres, etc.), are Linux-based.

Confusing WSL (a full separate Linux install) with Git Bash (a lighter POSIX-compatible layer on top of Windows) -- both give you a usable shell for this module, but they aren't the same thing under the hood.
topics.handsOn: Open a terminal (Git Bash, WSL, or any Linux/macOS terminal) and run all three commands above. Confirm you see real output for each, not an error.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain in one sentence why cloud/DevOps work assumes a Linux shell, and you have a working terminal open.

checks.q: Why does almost all cloud/server infrastructure default to Linux instead of Windows?
checks.a: Linux is free/open-source (no per-server licensing cost at scale), fully scriptable and automatable, and its multi-user process/permission model was built from the start for many services sharing one machine -- which is exactly the shape of cloud infrastructure.

keyTakeaways: A shell reads typed text commands and runs them -- it's the primary interface for servers, containers, and cloud infrastructure.
Nearly all cloud VM images and Docker base images run Linux, not Windows or macOS.
echo / whoami / pwd are a fast proof-of-life check in any new shell.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Open a terminal (Git Bash, WSL, or any Linux/macOS terminal) and run `echo "hello from the shell"`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: The exact text `hello from the shell` printed back — echo just repeats what you give it.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `pwd`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: A full path ending wherever your terminal opened — this is your proof-of-life check: if these three commands ran without errors, your shell works and you're ready for the rest of this module.
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If nothing happens or you see a syntax highlighting/autocomplete popup instead of output, you're probably typing into a text editor or your browser's address bar, not an actual terminal — this is the #1 mistake beginners hit here.

topics.title: Navigating the filesystem
topics.concept: Linux organizes everything -- files, directories, even devices -- into one single tree starting at the root, written `/`. `pwd` prints where you currently are; `ls` lists what's in the current directory (`ls -la` shows hidden files and details); `cd` changes directory. A path is either ABSOLUTE (starts with `/`, always means the same location no matter where you currently are, e.g. `/home/aditi/app`) or RELATIVE (doesn't start with `/`, interpreted from your CURRENT directory, e.g. `logs/error.log`). Two special relative names matter everywhere: `.` means "this directory" and `..` means "one directory up." Files or directories starting with `.` (like `.env` or `.git`) are HIDDEN by convention -- `ls` skips them unless you pass `-a`.
topics.analogy: An absolute path is like a full mailing address (works from anywhere in the world); a relative path is like saying "next door" or "upstairs" -- only meaningful given where you're currently standing. `..` is walking back out the front door of wherever you are; `.` is just pointing at your own feet.

examples.code:
pwd
mkdir myproject
cd myproject
pwd
mkdir logs
cd logs
pwd
cd ..
pwd
touch .env
ls -la
examples.note: Actually run: this exact sequence produces a nested `myproject/logs` directory, demonstrates absolute pwd output changing as you cd deeper and then back out with `..`, and shows `.env` appearing only once `ls -la` (not plain `ls`) is used, since dotfiles are hidden by default.

mistakes: Confusing a relative path with an absolute one -- `cd logs` only works if `logs` exists inside your CURRENT directory; from anywhere else, you need the full `/path/to/logs`.
Forgetting `-a` on `ls` and concluding a hidden config file (like `.env` or `.gitignore`) doesn't exist, when it's simply not shown by default.
Using `cd ../..` without checking `pwd` first and ending up two directories higher than intended -- always confirm your location with `pwd` after navigating.
topics.handsOn: Create a directory tree at least 2 levels deep, navigate into it using a relative path, print your location, navigate back out using `..`, and create one hidden file — then list it with and without `-a` to see the difference.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain the difference between an absolute and relative path, and you've navigated a multi-level directory tree using `cd`, `pwd`, and `..`.

checks.q: What's the difference between an absolute path and a relative path?
checks.a: An absolute path starts with `/` and always refers to the same location regardless of where you currently are. A relative path doesn't start with `/` and is interpreted relative to your current directory — the same relative path can point to different real locations depending on where you run it from.

keyTakeaways: Linux has one filesystem tree starting at `/`; `pwd`, `ls`, and `cd` are the core navigation commands.
Absolute paths always mean the same location; relative paths depend on your current directory.
`.` means the current directory, `..` means one level up, and dotfiles are hidden unless you pass `-a` to `ls`.

handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Your original path with `/myproject` added to the end — you moved using a RELATIVE path (just the folder name), which only works because `myproject` is inside where you already were.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `mkdir logs && cd logs && pwd`.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `cd ..` then `pwd`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Back to the `/myproject` path from step 1 — `..` always means one level up from wherever you currently are.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `touch .env` then plain `ls`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `.env` does NOT appear in the listing — files starting with `.` are hidden by default, not actually missing.
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If you don't see any output at all from `ls`, that's correct if this is a fresh folder with only the hidden `.env` file in it — hidden means hidden, not that ls is broken.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Now run `ls -a`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `.env` now appears, alongside `.` (this directory) and `..` (its parent) — `-a` is the flag that stops hiding dotfiles.

topics.title: Creating, copying, and deleting files
topics.concept: `touch file` creates an empty file (or updates its timestamp if it exists). `mkdir dir` creates a directory; `mkdir -p a/b/c` creates nested directories in one call, including any missing parents. `cp source dest` copies a file; `cp -r source dest` is required to copy a whole DIRECTORY recursively. `mv source dest` moves or renames (Linux treats renaming as "moving to a new name in the same place"). `rm file` deletes a file permanently -- there is no recycle bin. `rm -r dir` deletes a directory and everything inside it; `rm -rf dir` adds `-f` (force, suppress confirmation prompts) and is one of the most dangerous commands in Linux, since it deletes silently and irreversibly.
topics.analogy: `rm` is not like dragging a file to a Recycle Bin you can later restore from -- it's closer to shredding a physical document on the spot. `-rf` is handing someone the shredder AND telling them not to ask you first, which is exactly why it's the command every experienced engineer treats with real caution.

examples.code:
mkdir -p project/src/utils
touch project/src/utils/helpers.js
cp project/src/utils/helpers.js project/src/utils/helpers.backup.js
ls project/src/utils
mv project/src/utils/helpers.backup.js project/src/archive.js
ls project/src
rm project/src/archive.js
ls project/src
examples.note: Actually run: nested directories created in one `mkdir -p` call, a file copied (both copies coexist), then moved to a new location AND new name in one `mv` call (Linux doesn't distinguish moving from renaming), then deleted -- confirming afterward with `ls` that it's genuinely gone, not recoverable.

mistakes: Running `rm -rf` with a path that has a typo or an extra space (e.g. `rm -rf ~ /oldbuild` instead of `rm -rf ~/oldbuild`) -- the space makes it two separate arguments, and `rm -rf ~` would attempt to delete your entire home directory. Always double-check `-rf` commands before pressing Enter.
Trying `cp` on a directory without `-r` and getting an "omitting directory" error -- `cp` alone only copies files.
Assuming `mv` leaves a copy behind like `cp` does -- `mv` removes the file from its original location entirely.
topics.handsOn: Create a small nested directory structure with `mkdir -p`, populate it with a couple of files via `touch`, copy one, move/rename another, then delete one with plain `rm` (not `-rf`) and confirm with `ls` that it's gone.
topics.doneWhen: You can create nested directories in one command, distinguish `cp` from `mv`, and explain why `rm -rf` needs extra caution.

checks.q: Why is `rm -rf` considered one of the most dangerous commands in Linux?
checks.a: It deletes files and directories recursively (`-r`) without any confirmation prompt (`-f`, force) and there is no recycle bin to recover from — a typo in the path (like an accidental space) can delete far more than intended, permanently and silently.

keyTakeaways: `touch`/`mkdir -p`/`cp -r`/`mv`/`rm -rf` are the core file-management commands — `-r` (recursive) and `-f` (force) are the flags that make directory operations and deletions work, and also the ones that make mistakes expensive.
There is no recycle bin — `rm` is permanent.
`mv` both renames and relocates; Linux treats them as the same underlying operation.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `mkdir -p project/src/utils` then `touch project/src/utils/helpers.js`, then `ls project/src/utils`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `mkdir -p` created `project`, `project/src`, AND `project/src/utils` in one call even though none of them existed yet, and `helpers.js` now shows up inside the deepest one.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `cp project/src/utils/helpers.js project/src/utils/helpers.backup.js` then `ls project/src/utils` again.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Both `helpers.js` and `helpers.backup.js` now listed — `cp` leaves the original in place and creates a second, independent copy.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `mv project/src/utils/helpers.backup.js project/src/archive.js` then `ls project/src`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `archive.js` now sitting directly in `project/src` (not in `utils` anymore) — `mv` moved AND renamed it in one step, and it's gone from `utils` entirely.
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If you still see `helpers.backup.js` in the old location, double-check you used `mv` and not `cp` — unlike `cp`, `mv` never leaves the original behind.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `rm project/src/archive.js` then `ls project/src` to confirm.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `archive.js` no longer listed — plain `rm` on a single file is safe and reversible only via a backup, not via any undo command, which is exactly why the next step matters.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Before you ever run `rm -rf` for real, type out (don't run) the exact path you'd delete and read it back character by character, checking for stray spaces.
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: `rm -rf ~ /oldbuild` (with a space after `~`) deletes your ENTIRE home directory, not the `oldbuild` folder — this is the single most-cited real rm disaster, and it comes from a typo, not a misunderstanding of the command.

topics.title: Reading files from the terminal
topics.concept: `cat file` prints an entire file's contents to the terminal at once -- fine for short files, unwieldy for long ones. `head -n N file` shows just the first N lines; `tail -n N file` shows just the last N lines -- both are the standard way to peek at large log files without dumping the whole thing. `tail -f file` (follow) keeps the terminal open and prints new lines AS they're appended -- the standard way to watch a live log file in real time on a running server. `less file` opens a file in a scrollable, searchable pager without loading the whole thing into your terminal's scrollback -- the right tool for files too large to comfortably `cat`.
topics.analogy: `cat` is dumping an entire filing cabinet drawer onto your desk at once. `head`/`tail` are peeking at just the top or bottom folder. `tail -f` is standing at the fax machine watching new pages print out live. `less` is flipping through the drawer one page at a time with a search function, without ever removing anything from the cabinet.

examples.code:
printf 'line1\nline2\nline3\nline4\nline5\n' > sample.log
cat sample.log
echo '--- head -n 2 ---'
head -n 2 sample.log
echo '--- tail -n 2 ---'
tail -n 2 sample.log
examples.note: Actually run: cat prints all 5 lines; head -n 2 shows only line1/line2; tail -n 2 shows only line4/line5 — confirming each command's real, distinct output on the exact same file.

mistakes: Using `cat` on a multi-gigabyte log file and flooding your terminal — `head`, `tail`, or `less` are the correct tools once a file is more than a screenful.
Forgetting `-f` on `tail` when trying to watch a live-updating log — plain `tail` only shows a snapshot at the moment you ran it, not ongoing updates.
Trying to edit a file by piping `cat` output somewhere — `cat` is for reading/concatenating, not editing; that's the next lesson's job.
topics.handsOn: Create a text file with at least 10 lines. View the whole thing with `cat`, then just the first 3 lines with `head -n 3`, then just the last 3 with `tail -n 3`. If you have a long-running process available, try `tail -f` on a file it's writing to.
topics.doneWhen: You can choose the right command (`cat`/`head`/`tail`/`less`) for a given file-reading situation and explain why `tail -f` is used for live logs.

checks.q: You need to watch a server's log file update in real time as requests come in. Which command, and why?
checks.a: `tail -f logfile` — the `-f` (follow) flag keeps the terminal open and prints new lines as they're appended, rather than showing only a one-time snapshot like plain `cat` or `tail` would.

keyTakeaways: `cat` dumps a whole file; `head`/`tail` show just the start/end; `less` lets you scroll/search without loading everything.
`tail -f` is the standard way to watch a live log file update in real time.
Choosing the right reading command matters once files get large — `cat`-ing a huge log file is a real, avoidable mistake.

topics.title: Editing files in the terminal
topics.concept: Sooner or later you'll need to edit a config file directly on a server with no GUI editor available — that's what terminal text editors are for. `nano` is the beginner-friendly choice: it shows its keyboard shortcuts on screen at all times (`^O` to save/"write out", `^X` to exit), so there's nothing to memorize up front. `vim` (or its predecessor `vi`) is far more powerful and near-universally available on any Linux system, but it's MODAL — it starts in "normal mode" (keys are commands, not text input) and you must explicitly press `i` to enter "insert mode" before typing text, then `Esc` to leave insert mode, then `:wq` to write and quit (or `:q!` to quit WITHOUT saving). This modal design is the single most common beginner stumbling block with vim.
topics.analogy: `nano` is like a whiteboard with the instructions written in the corner — you can just start writing. `vim` is like a professional camera with full manual controls: far more capable once you know it, but if you don't know that you first have to switch it out of "viewing mode" into "shooting mode," you'll just stand there confused about why pressing buttons doesn't do what you expect.

examples.code:
nano config.yaml
# type your changes, then:
# Ctrl+O  (write out / save)
# Enter   (confirm filename)
# Ctrl+X  (exit)
examples.note: Conceptual walkthrough, not run in this non-interactive shell -- nano is a full-screen interactive program, so its behavior can't be demonstrated via a single non-interactive command execution the way `cat`/`ls` can. Verified against nano's official documented keybindings.

examples.code:
vim config.yaml
# press i          -> enter INSERT mode, now typing works
# (make your edits)
# press Esc        -> back to NORMAL mode
# type :wq         -> write (save) and quit
# (or :q!          -> quit WITHOUT saving, if you want to discard changes)
examples.note: Conceptual walkthrough, not run in this non-interactive shell, for the same reason as above -- verified against Vim's official documentation. The single most important thing to remember as a beginner: if vim seems to be ignoring your typing, you are almost certainly still in NORMAL mode and need to press `i` first.

mistakes: Opening vim, typing immediately, and getting confused when letters trigger commands instead of appearing as text — you're still in normal mode; press `i` first.
Not knowing `:q!` exists and feeling stuck inside vim with unwanted changes — `:q!` discards changes and quits; this is the single most useful vim escape-hatch to memorize.
Trying to use arrow keys or a mouse to click into a specific line in a bare SSH session with no GUI — terminal editors are keyboard-only by design.
topics.handsOn: Open a file in nano, make an edit, save with Ctrl+O then exit with Ctrl+X. Separately, open a file in vim, press `i`, type something, press `Esc`, then save and quit with `:wq`. Then open vim again, make a change you don't want to keep, and discard it with `:q!`.
topics.doneWhen: You can open, edit, and save a file in both nano and vim, and you know vim's `i` / `Esc` / `:wq` / `:q!` sequence by heart.

checks.q: You're in vim and your keypresses aren't typing text — they seem to be running commands instead. What's happening and how do you fix it?
checks.a: You're in NORMAL mode, not INSERT mode — vim is modal, and typing only inserts text once you're in insert mode. Press `i` to enter insert mode, then type normally; press `Esc` to return to normal mode when done.

keyTakeaways: nano is beginner-friendly with on-screen shortcuts (Ctrl+O to save, Ctrl+X to exit).
vim is modal — press `i` for insert mode before typing, `Esc` to leave it, `:wq` to save and quit, `:q!` to discard and quit.
Terminal editors are keyboard-only — there's no mouse-click-to-position-cursor on a bare server session.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `nano test.txt`, type a line of text, then press Ctrl+O, Enter, then Ctrl+X.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: You're back at your normal shell prompt, and running `cat test.txt` afterward shows the line you typed — nano's on-screen shortcuts (shown at the bottom the whole time) are there so you never have to memorize them up front.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `vim test.txt`. Before typing anything, press `i`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `-- INSERT --` appears at the bottom of the screen — this is vim confirming you can now type normally.
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If you type before pressing `i` and letters seem to vanish or trigger weird jumps, you were still in NORMAL mode, where keys are commands, not text. This is the single most common vim confusion — press Esc, then `i`, and start again.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Type a short line, press Esc, then type `:wq` and press Enter.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Back at your shell prompt; `cat test.txt` shows your new line was saved — `:wq` means write (save) then quit.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Open vim again (`vim test.txt`), press `i`, type something you do NOT want to keep, press Esc, then type `:q!` and press Enter.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Back at your shell prompt with no save prompt or error — `:q!` discards your changes and exits, unlike `:wq`. This is the escape hatch worth memorizing before you ever get stuck in vim for real.

topics.title: Permissions and ownership
topics.concept: Every Linux file has an OWNER (a user) and a GROUP, plus three permission classes checked in order — owner, group, and everyone else ("other") — each with independent READ (r), WRITE (w), and EXECUTE (x) bits. `ls -l` shows this as a 10-character string like `-rwxr-xr--`: the first character is the file type, then three groups of rwx for owner/group/other. `chmod` changes permissions, either SYMBOLICALLY (`chmod u+x file` adds execute for the owner, `chmod go-w file` removes write for group and other) or NUMERICALLY (`chmod 755 file` sets owner=rwx(7), group=rx(5), other=rx(5) — each digit is the sum of r=4, w=2, x=1). `chown user:group file` changes who owns a file. `chmod 777` (everyone can read/write/execute) is a common but genuinely dangerous shortcut — it means literally any user or process on the system can modify or execute that file.
topics.analogy: Permission bits are like a building's key system: the owner has a master key (rwx), the group has a shared department key (their own rwx), and everyone else has whatever access the front desk decides to leave for the public (other's rwx). `chmod 777` is leaving the building's front door propped open with a master key taped to it — convenient in the moment, and a real security problem the moment anyone untrusted walks by.

examples.code:
touch deploy.sh
ls -l deploy.sh
chmod 755 deploy.sh
ls -l deploy.sh
chmod u+x,go-w deploy.sh
ls -l deploy.sh
examples.note: Doc-grounded, not fully demonstrable in this authoring environment: the exact syntax (`chmod 755`, `chmod u+x,go-w`) is correct per GNU coreutils' chmod documentation and standard Linux behavior, but this content was authored on a Windows filesystem (NTFS) via Git Bash, where chmod's numeric effect is not faithfully reproduced the way it is on a real Linux (ext4/xfs) filesystem — running this same sequence on a real Linux box or server is genuinely required to see the permission bits actually change in `ls -l`'s output.

mistakes: Running `chmod 777` on a web-facing file or script "to make an error go away" — this is one of the most common real security misconfigurations; the actual fix is almost always the correct, narrower permission (e.g. `755` for an executable, `644` for a regular file), not "everyone gets everything."
Confusing numeric chmod digits — remembering 7=rwx (4+2+1), 5=r-x (4+0+1), 6=rw- (4+2+0), 0=--- is worth memorizing rather than guessing.

Forgetting that changing a SCRIPT file's content doesn't restore its execute bit if it was removed — permissions and content are independent; a freshly-copied script often loses its execute bit and needs `chmod +x` again.
topics.handsOn: On a real Linux machine or VM (not required to be this authoring environment), create a file, view its permissions with `ls -l`, change them with a numeric chmod, then again with a symbolic chmod, confirming the `ls -l` output changes each time. Then explain in your own words why `chmod 777` is risky.
topics.doneWhen: You can read a 10-character permission string from `ls -l` and explain what each part means, and you can convert between numeric and symbolic chmod syntax.

checks.q: What do the three permission classes shown in `ls -l`'s `-rwxr-xr--` represent, and what does chmod 755 set them to?
checks.a: The three classes are owner, group, and other (everyone else), each with read/write/execute bits. `chmod 755` sets owner to rwx (7 = 4+2+1), and group and other to r-x (5 = 4+0+1) — the owner can read, write, and execute; everyone else can only read and execute, not modify.

keyTakeaways: Every file has an owner, a group, and other — each with independent read/write/execute permissions, shown as a 10-character string in `ls -l`.
chmod changes permissions either numerically (chmod 755) or symbolically (chmod u+x); chown changes ownership.
chmod 777 (everyone gets full access) is a common but genuinely dangerous shortcut, not a real fix for a permission error.

handsOnSteps.instruction: On a real Linux machine, VM, or container (chmod's numeric effect doesn't reproduce faithfully on Windows/NTFS, even via Git Bash), run `touch deploy.sh` then `ls -l deploy.sh`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: A line starting with something like `-rw-r--r--` — the leading `-` means 'regular file', and the next 9 characters are owner/group/other permissions, none of which include execute (`x`) yet.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `chmod 755 deploy.sh` then `ls -l deploy.sh` again.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: The permission string changes to `-rwxr-xr-x` — owner now has read+write+execute (7), group and other have read+execute (5 each).

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `chmod u+x,go-w deploy.sh` then `ls -l` once more.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: The string reflects the symbolic change: owner keeps execute (was already set), group and other lose write if they had it — symbolic chmod adjusts specific bits without restating the whole permission set the way numeric chmod does.

handsOnSteps.instruction: In your own words, write one sentence explaining why `chmod 777` on a web-facing file is risky.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Something covering: 777 gives EVERY user on the system full read/write/execute — including write access for people who should never be able to modify that file. The fix is almost always a narrower, correct permission (755 or 644), not 'everyone gets everything'.

topics.title: Processes and job control
topics.concept: Every running program is a PROCESS with a unique PID (process ID). `ps` lists running processes (`ps aux` shows all processes system-wide, with owner and resource usage); `top` shows a live, auto-refreshing view sorted by resource usage. Appending `&` to a command runs it in the BACKGROUND, freeing your terminal immediately; `jobs` lists your shell's current background jobs, and `fg`/`bg` bring a job to the foreground or resume it in the background. `kill PID` sends a termination SIGNAL to a process (by default `SIGTERM`, a polite "please stop" the process can catch and clean up after) — `kill -9 PID` sends `SIGKILL`, which the operating system enforces immediately and the process cannot intercept or ignore, a last resort when a process won't respond to a normal `kill`. Every command also returns an EXIT CODE when it finishes — `0` means success, any nonzero value signals a specific kind of failure — and shell scripts routinely check `$?` (the previous command's exit code) to decide what to do next.
topics.analogy: A process is like a specific task someone is doing in a shared office. `ps`/`top` are walking the floor to see who's doing what and how much desk space (CPU/memory) they're using. `&` is telling a colleague "go handle that in the next room, don't block my desk." A normal `kill` is politely asking someone to wrap up and leave; `kill -9` is security escorting them out immediately, mid-sentence, without letting them finish what they were doing.

examples.code:
sleep 30 &
JOB_PID=$!
echo "started background job with PID $JOB_PID"
jobs
kill $JOB_PID
sleep 1
jobs
examples.note: Actually run: sleep 30 launched in the background with &, $! captured its PID, jobs confirmed it running, kill sent it a termination signal, and a second jobs call confirmed it terminated — a real, observable process lifecycle, not just a description of one.

examples.code:
true; echo "true exit code: $?"
false; echo "false exit code: $?"
ls /nonexistent-path 2>/dev/null; echo "missing-path exit code: $?"
examples.note: Actually run: `true` always exits 0 (success), `false` always exits 1 (generic failure), and `ls` on a nonexistent path exits 2 — confirming that different failure modes really do produce different nonzero codes, which is exactly what scripts branch on via `$?`.

mistakes: Reaching for `kill -9` as a first resort — it prevents the process from cleaning up (closing files, finishing a write, releasing a lock), which can corrupt state; a plain `kill` (SIGTERM) should almost always be tried first.
Forgetting a long-running command needs `&` before starting it, and then being stuck unable to type further commands until it finishes or you background it after the fact.

Ignoring a command's exit code in a script and assuming success just because it "looked like it ran" — always check `$?` (or use `set -e`, covered next lesson) when a later step depends on an earlier one having actually succeeded.
topics.handsOn: Start a long-running command in the background with `&`, confirm it's running with `jobs`, then terminate it with `kill`. Separately, run one command you know will succeed and one you know will fail, checking `$?` after each.
topics.doneWhen: You can start, list, and terminate a background job, and you can explain the difference between a normal `kill` and `kill -9`.

checks.q: Why should you try a normal `kill` before reaching for `kill -9`?
checks.a: A normal `kill` sends SIGTERM, which the process can catch and use to clean up gracefully (closing files, finishing writes, releasing locks) before exiting. `kill -9` sends SIGKILL, which the OS enforces immediately with no chance for the process to clean up — this can corrupt state, so it's a last resort, not a first move.

keyTakeaways: Every running program is a process with a PID; `ps`/`top` show what's running, `&`/`jobs`/`fg`/`bg` control background jobs.
`kill` sends SIGTERM (a polite request the process can handle); `kill -9` sends SIGKILL (immediate, un-catchable termination) — try the polite version first.
Every command returns a numeric exit code ($?) — 0 means success, nonzero means some specific kind of failure — and scripts should check it before assuming a prior step worked.

topics.title: Installing software with a package manager
topics.concept: Instead of manually downloading and compiling software, Linux distributions use a PACKAGE MANAGER to install, update, and remove software along with its dependencies automatically. Debian/Ubuntu-based systems (by far the most common base for cloud VM images and Docker images) use `apt`: `sudo apt update` refreshes the list of available package versions, `sudo apt install nginx` installs a package, `sudo apt upgrade` updates installed packages, `sudo apt remove nginx` uninstalls one. Red Hat/CentOS/Fedora-based systems use `dnf` (or the older `yum`) with equivalent subcommands (`dnf install`, `dnf update`). `sudo` ("superuser do") temporarily runs a single command with administrator privileges — required for most package-manager operations, since installing software system-wide needs elevated permission.
topics.analogy: A package manager is like ordering from a supplier's official catalog instead of sourcing every part yourself: you ask for "nginx" by name, and it automatically pulls in every dependency that package needs, checks for conflicts, and gives you a clean way to remove it later — versus manually downloading source code, figuring out what libraries it needs, and hoping nothing conflicts with what's already installed.

examples.code:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install nginx
nginx -v
sudo apt remove nginx
examples.note: Doc-grounded, not executed in this authoring environment (no Debian/Ubuntu apt package manager available here) -- this exact command sequence matches Ubuntu's and Debian's own official package-management documentation and is standard, low-risk practice on any real Ubuntu/Debian server or cloud VM.

mistakes: Running `apt install` without `sudo update` first and getting an outdated or missing package because your local package list is stale.
Mixing package managers on the same system (e.g. installing the same software via both `apt` and a manual download) — this can create version conflicts that are confusing to debug later.

Assuming every Linux distribution uses the same package manager — Debian/Ubuntu use `apt`, Red Hat/Fedora/CentOS use `dnf`/`yum`, and the two are not interchangeable; always check which family a given server/image is based on.
topics.handsOn: On a real Ubuntu/Debian machine, VM, or Docker container (e.g. `docker run -it ubuntu bash`), run `apt update` then install and remove one small package (like `curl` or `tree`), confirming it works before and fails after removal.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what a package manager does and why `sudo` is required for it, and you know which package manager family (apt vs dnf/yum) matches a given Linux distribution.

checks.q: Why does installing software with apt typically require `sudo`?
checks.a: Installing software system-wide (so any user on the machine can run it) requires writing to protected system directories, which normal (non-administrator) users can't do. `sudo` temporarily elevates just that one command to administrator privileges to allow it.

keyTakeaways: Package managers (apt for Debian/Ubuntu, dnf/yum for Red Hat family) install software plus its dependencies automatically, and let you update or remove it cleanly later.
`sudo apt update` refreshes available package info; `install`/`upgrade`/`remove` are the core lifecycle commands.
Debian/Ubuntu-based images are the most common base for cloud VMs and Docker images — apt is the package manager you'll use most in this path.

handsOnSteps.instruction: On a real Ubuntu/Debian machine, VM, or container (e.g. `docker run -it ubuntu bash`) — not required to be this authoring environment — run `sudo apt update`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: A series of lines fetching package lists ending in something like `Reading package lists... Done` — this refreshes what versions are available before you install anything.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `sudo apt install curl` (or `tree` if curl is already present), then confirm it works, e.g. `curl --version`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Real version output — the package is now genuinely usable, not just 'installed' in name.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `sudo apt remove curl`, then try `curl --version` again.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: A 'command not found' error — confirming removal genuinely took the software away rather than just hiding it.
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If install fails with permission errors, make sure you're using `sudo` — package managers modify system-wide locations that a normal user account can't write to directly.

topics.title: Shell scripting basics
topics.concept: A shell SCRIPT is just a text file of commands run in sequence, saved with a `#!/usr/bin/env bash` SHEBANG line at the top (tells the OS which interpreter runs the file) and made executable with `chmod +x script.sh`. Variables are assigned with `NAME=value` (no spaces around `=`) and read with `$NAME`; `$1`, `$2`, etc. are POSITIONAL ARGUMENTS passed on the command line, and `${1:-default}` supplies a fallback if none was given. `if [ condition ]; then ... else ... fi` branches on a condition; `for item in a b c; do ... done` loops over a list. `set -euo pipefail` at the top of a script is a widely-recommended safety habit: `-e` exits immediately if any command fails, `-u` errors on any unset variable instead of silently treating it as empty, and `pipefail` makes a pipeline fail if ANY command in it fails, not just the last one.
topics.analogy: A shell script is a written recipe instead of cooking from memory each time: the shebang says which kitchen's conventions to follow, positional arguments are substitutable ingredients ("serves however many people you tell it to"), and `set -euo pipefail` is the equivalent of "stop cooking immediately and tell someone the moment anything goes wrong" instead of pushing ahead and serving a dish that's quietly missing an ingredient.

examples.code:
cat > deploy.sh << 'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

ENVIRONMENT="${1:-staging}"
echo "Deploying to: $ENVIRONMENT"

if [ "$ENVIRONMENT" = "production" ]; then
  echo "Running production safety checks..."
else
  echo "Skipping safety checks for non-prod environment."
fi

for service in api worker scheduler; do
  echo "  -> deploying $service"
done

echo "Deploy to $ENVIRONMENT complete."
EOF
chmod +x deploy.sh
./deploy.sh
./deploy.sh production
examples.note: Actually run, both ways: with no argument it defaults to "staging" (via ${1:-staging}) and skips the safety-check branch; called again with "production" as $1, it takes the if-branch and prints the safety-check line instead -- confirming positional arguments, the default-value fallback, and the if/else branch all behave exactly as described, on the same script.

mistakes: Putting spaces around `=` in a variable assignment (`NAME = value`) — bash parses this as running a command called `NAME` with arguments `=` and `value`, not an assignment; it must be `NAME=value` with no spaces.
Forgetting `set -e` and having a script silently continue after an earlier command failed, producing confusing downstream errors instead of stopping immediately at the real point of failure.
Forgetting `chmod +x` on a new script and getting a "permission denied" error when trying to run it with `./script.sh`.
topics.handsOn: Write a small script with a shebang, one variable, one positional-argument default, an if/else branch, and a for loop — like the deploy.sh example. Make it executable and run it twice: once with no argument, once passing an argument, and confirm the behavior differs correctly.
topics.doneWhen: You can write, make executable, and run a bash script that uses a variable, a positional argument with a default, an if/else branch, and a for loop.

checks.q: What does `set -euo pipefail` do at the top of a bash script, and why is it a recommended habit?
checks.a: `-e` exits the script immediately if any command fails, `-u` errors on any unset/undefined variable instead of silently treating it as empty, and `pipefail` makes a piped command chain fail if any command in the pipe fails (not just the last one). Together they make scripts fail loudly and immediately at the real point of a problem, instead of silently continuing with bad state.

keyTakeaways: A script is a shebang-headed, chmod +x'd text file of sequential commands — variables use NAME=value (no spaces) and are read with $NAME.
Positional arguments ($1, $2...) with `${1:-default}` fallbacks let a script adapt to how it's called.
`set -euo pipefail` is a standard safety habit: fail fast and loudly on errors, unset variables, or failed pipeline stages, rather than continuing silently.

Add an if/else: if `[ "$ENVIRONMENT" = "production" ]`, echo a safety-check message; else echo a 'skipping' message. Then add a `for service in api worker scheduler; do echo "  -> deploying $service"; done` loop.
Run `chmod +x deploy.sh`, then run it twice: `./deploy.sh` (no argument) and `./deploy.sh production`.

handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If you get `permission denied` when running `./deploy.sh`, you skipped `chmod +x` — the file needs its execute bit set before `./` can run it directly.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Deliberately add a space around one `=` in your script (e.g. change `ENVIRONMENT="${1:-staging}"` to `ENVIRONMENT = "${1:-staging}"`) and run it again.

title: Networking Fundamentals for Ops
why: Every service you'll ever deploy, containerize, or orchestrate talks to other services over a network -- and when something breaks in production, it's very often a networking problem (DNS, a closed port, a misconfigured firewall rule, an overloaded backend). This module builds the mental model and the debugging tools (curl, DNS lookups, ports) you'll lean on constantly in every module ahead.

topics.title: How two computers talk: the client-server model
topics.concept: Almost every network interaction follows the CLIENT-SERVER model: a CLIENT (your browser, an app, another service) initiates a request, and a SERVER (a program listening for connections) responds. Every device on a network has an IP ADDRESS -- a numeric identifier (IPv4 looks like `93.184.216.34`; IPv6 looks like `2606:4700::6810:84e5`) that's how packets know where to go, the same way a postal address routes a letter. A PUBLIC IP address is reachable from the internet; a PRIVATE IP address (ranges like `10.x.x.x`, `192.168.x.x`, `172.16.x.x`-`172.31.x.x`) only works within a local network and is NOT directly reachable from outside it -- this is exactly why cloud VMs typically have both a private IP (for internal traffic) and a public IP (for internet-facing traffic).
topics.analogy: The client-server model is a customer (client) walking up to a service counter and making a request, with staff (the server) responding -- the counter doesn't wander around finding customers, it waits and responds to whoever approaches. An IP address is a street address: a private IP is like an internal apartment number only meaningful inside one building, while a public IP is the building's actual street address, reachable from anywhere in the city.

examples.code: curl -s -o /dev/null -w "Status: %{http_code}\nTime: %{time_total}s\n" https://api.github.com
examples.note: Actually run: this made a real client request to GitHub's API server and printed the real HTTP status code (200) and round-trip time -- a concrete client-server exchange, not a diagram.

mistakes: Trying to reach a server's PRIVATE IP address from outside its own network -- private IP ranges are non-routable on the public internet by design; you need the server's public IP (or a VPN/tunnel into the private network) instead.
Assuming 'server' means a physical machine in a closet -- a server is just any program listening for and responding to connections; a laptop running a local dev server is a server in this sense too.
Confusing IPv4 (`93.184.216.34`, 4 numbers 0-255) with IPv6 (`2606:4700::6810:84e5`, hex groups separated by colons) -- they're different addressing schemes and not interchangeable in configuration.
topics.handsOn: Run `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://api.github.com` and confirm you get a real status code back. Then look up your own machine's local network IP (`ipconfig` on Windows, `ip addr` on Linux) and identify whether it falls in a private range (10.x, 172.16-31.x, or 192.168.x).
topics.doneWhen: You can explain the client-server model in one sentence and distinguish a private IP address from a public one.

checks.q: Why can't you reach a cloud VM's private IP address directly from your home internet connection?
checks.a: Private IP ranges (like 10.x.x.x or 192.168.x.x) are non-routable on the public internet by design -- they only have meaning within their own local/virtual network. To reach a VM from outside, you need its public IP address (or a VPN/tunnel that bridges into the private network).

keyTakeaways: Networking follows a client-server model: clients initiate requests, servers listen and respond.
Every networked device has an IP address; private IPs (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x) only work within a local network, public IPs are reachable from the internet.
Cloud VMs typically have both -- a private IP for internal traffic, a public IP for internet-facing traffic.

handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `Status: 200` — a real client (curl) made a real request and got a real response back from GitHub's server, the exact client-server exchange this lesson describes.

topics.title: TCP vs UDP: reliable vs fast
topics.concept: Below HTTP and other application protocols sits the TRANSPORT layer, almost always either TCP or UDP. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is CONNECTION-ORIENTED and RELIABLE: it performs a three-step 'handshake' (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) before sending data, guarantees packets arrive in order, and automatically retransmits anything lost -- at the cost of extra overhead and latency. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is CONNECTIONLESS: it just fires packets with no handshake, no ordering guarantee, and no automatic retransmission -- faster and lower-overhead, but the application itself must handle any lost or out-of-order data if that matters. Most things you build (HTTP/HTTPS APIs, databases, SSH) use TCP because correctness matters more than raw speed; UDP is chosen when speed matters more than perfect delivery (video/voice calls, DNS lookups, online gaming) since a dropped packet there is better handled by skipping it than by stalling everything to retransmit it.
topics.analogy: TCP is a registered, tracked courier delivery: you confirm the recipient is ready before sending (handshake), every package is numbered and reassembled in order, and a lost package gets automatically resent. UDP is dropping postcards in a mailbox: fast and simple, but nobody confirms delivery, and if one goes missing, nobody automatically sends a replacement -- fine for something like a live video frame (a dropped one is just briefly skipped), unavoidably bad for something like a bank transfer.

examples.code:
# TCP: curl over HTTPS uses a TCP connection underneath -- the handshake happens before any HTTP data is exchanged
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "Connect time (TCP handshake + TLS): %{time_connect}s\nTotal time: %{time_total}s\n" https://api.github.com
examples.note: Actually run: curl's %{time_connect} timing metric measures exactly the TCP connection setup phase (including the handshake) that happens before any actual HTTP request/response data is sent -- a real, measurable illustration of TCP's connection-oriented nature.

mistakes: Assuming TCP is always the 'better' choice because it's reliable -- for real-time media (video calls, live game state), UDP's lower latency usually matters more than perfect delivery, since a stale retransmitted packet is often worse than a briefly dropped one.

Forgetting that DNS lookups themselves typically use UDP (for speed, since a query is small and a quick retry is cheap) but fall back to TCP for larger responses -- DNS is a common example that uses both.

Confusing 'connectionless' (UDP) with 'insecure' -- UDP can absolutely be encrypted (e.g. QUIC, which HTTP/3 is built on, runs over UDP with its own encryption); connection-oriented and encrypted are independent properties.
topics.handsOn: Run the curl timing example above and note the connect-time value. Then list 2 real applications you use daily that likely rely on UDP (hint: video calls, live multiplayer games) and 2 that rely on TCP (hint: loading a webpage, SSH-ing into a server), and explain why each made that choice.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain the core tradeoff between TCP and UDP and give a real example of when each is the right choice.

checks.q: Why would a live video call typically use UDP instead of TCP?
checks.a: TCP guarantees ordered, lossless delivery by retransmitting lost packets and waiting for them -- but for live video, a delayed-but-eventually-correct frame is worse than briefly skipping a dropped one. UDP's lower latency and lack of retransmission stalls make it the better fit when timeliness matters more than perfect delivery.

keyTakeaways: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable (handshake, ordering, automatic retransmission) at the cost of overhead and latency.
UDP is connectionless and fast, with no delivery/ordering guarantees -- the application must handle loss itself if it matters.
Most correctness-sensitive traffic (HTTP APIs, databases, SSH) uses TCP; latency-sensitive traffic (video/voice, DNS, gaming) often uses UDP.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "Connect time: %{time_connect}s\nTotal time: %{time_total}s\n" https://api.github.com`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Two small numbers, both under a second on a normal connection — `time_connect` is specifically the TCP handshake (plus TLS) completing BEFORE any HTTP data moves at all.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write down 2 apps you use daily that likely run over UDP (hint: anything real-time — video calls, live multiplayer) and 2 that rely on TCP (hint: loading a webpage, SSH).

For each of the 4, write one sentence explaining why that protocol fits: does this app care more about EVERY packet arriving correctly (TCP), or about the newest data arriving FAST even if a packet is dropped (UDP)?
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: The core reasoning: a video call losing one frame briefly is fine (UDP — don't wait to retransmit it, just show the next one); a webpage missing a byte of HTML is not fine (TCP — retransmit until it's complete, even if slower).

topics.title: HTTP and the request-response cycle
topics.concept: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the application-layer protocol nearly every web API and website is built on, running on top of TCP. Every HTTP exchange is a REQUEST (method + path + headers + optional body) followed by a RESPONSE (status code + headers + optional body). The main METHODS are GET (retrieve data, no side effects expected), POST (create something new / submit data), PUT (replace a resource entirely), PATCH (partially update a resource), and DELETE (remove a resource). STATUS CODES are grouped by their first digit: 2xx = success (200 OK, 201 Created), 3xx = redirect (301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found), 4xx = client error (400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found), 5xx = server error (500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable). HTTPS is HTTP wrapped in TLS encryption -- same request/response model, but the connection itself is encrypted so an eavesdropper on the network can't read the contents.
topics.analogy: An HTTP request is a filled-out request form at a counter: the method is which type of form you're submitting (asking for something vs. submitting new information vs. replacing an existing record vs. deleting one), and the status code is the stamped reply -- 2xx is 'approved,' 4xx is 'your form was wrong,' 5xx is 'our office made a mistake,' not yours.

examples.note: Actually run against GitHub's real public API: a plain GET returned 200 (success); a POST attempting to create a repo with no authentication/body returned 404 (GitHub's API deliberately returns 404 rather than 401 for some unauthenticated write attempts, to avoid revealing resource existence); requesting a nonsense path also returned 404 -- real status codes from a real server, not simulated.

mistakes: Treating all 4xx errors as "my code is broken" without checking WHICH 4xx -- 401 (not authenticated), 403 (authenticated but not permitted), and 404 (doesn't exist) point to very different fixes.
Assuming a 500 error means the client did something wrong -- 5xx always means the SERVER failed to handle an otherwise-valid request; the fix is on the server side, not the client's.
Using GET for an action that changes data (like `GET /delete-user?id=5`) -- GET is expected to be side-effect-free and safely repeatable/cacheable; state changes belong in POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE.
topics.handsOn: Using curl, make a GET request to a real public API (e.g. `https://api.github.com`) and print just the status code. Then request a path you know doesn't exist on that same API and compare the status code. Look up what 401 vs 403 vs 404 each specifically mean.
topics.doneWhen: You can name the 5 main HTTP methods and their intent, and explain the difference between a 4xx and a 5xx status code.

checks.q: A client gets a 403 response. What does that specifically mean, versus a 401?
checks.a: 403 (Forbidden) means the server understood who's asking (they may even be authenticated) but is refusing to allow this specific action -- a permissions problem. 401 (Unauthorized) means the server doesn't know who's asking at all -- an authentication problem, not a permissions one.

keyTakeaways: HTTP requests have a method (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE), and responses have a status code grouped by first digit (2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error).
HTTPS is HTTP encrypted via TLS -- same request/response model, encrypted transport.
4xx errors point to a problem with the request itself (auth, permissions, bad input); 5xx errors mean the server failed to handle an otherwise-valid request.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "GET status: %{http_code}\n" https://api.github.com`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `GET status: 200` — a successful request/response.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "POST status: %{http_code}\n" -X POST https://api.github.com/repos`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `POST status: 404` — an unauthenticated write attempt; GitHub's API deliberately returns 404 rather than 401 here to avoid revealing what exists.
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If you expected 401 and got 404 instead, that's not a bug in your curl command — some APIs intentionally obscure resource existence from unauthenticated callers. Always check the specific API's own docs rather than assuming one universal convention.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "Status: %{http_code}\n" https://api.github.com/this-path-does-not-exist-xyz`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `Status: 404` — this time for the expected reason: the path genuinely doesn't exist.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write one sentence each for 401, 403, and 404: what specifically does each mean, and what's the fix?
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: 401 = not authenticated (fix: log in / send credentials). 403 = authenticated but not permitted (fix: needs different permissions, not different credentials). 404 = doesn't exist at all (fix: check the URL/resource, not auth).

topics.title: Ports and sockets
topics.concept: An IP address gets a packet to the right MACHINE; a PORT (a number 0-65535) gets it to the right PROGRAM/service running on that machine. Well-known ports have conventional assignments: 22 = SSH, 80 = HTTP, 443 = HTTPS, 5432 = PostgreSQL, 3306 = MySQL -- conventions, not hard rules, but deviating from them requires explicitly telling clients the nonstandard port. A SOCKET is the combination of IP address + port + protocol that identifies one specific network connection endpoint. Critically, only ONE process can BIND to (listen on) a given port on a given IP at a time -- if you try to start a second server on a port already in use, the operating system will refuse with an "address already in use" error, which is one of the most common real deployment errors.
topics.analogy: If an IP address is a building's street address, a port is the specific apartment/suite number within it -- mail (traffic) reaches the right building via the address, then the right occupant via the unit number. Only one tenant can hold a given unit number at a time, which is exactly why two processes can't both listen on the same port simultaneously.

examples.code:
python3 -c "
import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.bind(('127.0.0.1', 8765))
s.listen(1)
print('Bound successfully to port 8765')
s2 = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
try:
    s2.bind(('127.0.0.1', 8765))
    print('unexpectedly succeeded')
except OSError as e:
    print(f'Second bind to same port failed as expected: {e}')
s.close()
"
examples.note: Actually run: the first socket successfully binds to port 8765; a second socket attempting to bind to the exact same IP+port genuinely fails with a real OS-level 'address already in use' error -- this is precisely the error you'll hit if you accidentally try to start two servers on the same port.

mistakes: Seeing "address already in use" and assuming your code is broken, rather than checking whether an earlier instance of the same server is still running on that port (a very common cause during local development).

Hardcoding a well-known port's assumed service (e.g. assuming anything on port 443 is definitely a legitimate HTTPS server) -- port numbers are convention, not proof of what's actually listening there.

Forgetting that a firewall can block a port even if a service is correctly listening on it -- "connection refused" (nothing listening) and "connection timed out" (something, likely a firewall, is silently dropping the traffic) point to different problems.
topics.handsOn: Run the Python socket example above and confirm the second bind genuinely fails. Then look up (or recall) which port your own local dev server runs on, and check whether it matches one of the well-known conventional ports.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what a port is, why only one process can bind to a given port at a time, and what "address already in use" actually means.

checks.q: You start your app's server and get an 'address already in use' error. What's the most likely real-world cause?
checks.a: Another process -- very often an earlier instance of the same server that didn't shut down cleanly -- is already bound to (listening on) that exact port. Only one process can bind to a given IP+port combination at a time; the fix is usually to stop the other process or use a different port.

keyTakeaways: An IP address routes to a machine; a port routes to a specific program on that machine. Well-known ports (22, 80, 443, etc.) are conventions.
A socket is the IP + port + protocol combination identifying one connection endpoint.
Only one process can bind to a given port at a time -- "address already in use" is the OS enforcing exactly that.

topics.title: DNS: turning names into addresses
topics.concept: DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names (`github.com`) into the numeric IP addresses computers actually route traffic to -- effectively the internet's phone book. A DNS lookup RESOLVES a name by querying a chain of servers (root -> TLD -> authoritative nameserver) until it finds the answer, though in practice results are cached at multiple layers (your OS, your router, your ISP) so most lookups are fast and don't traverse the whole chain every time. The main RECORD TYPES: an `A` record maps a name to an IPv4 address; `AAAA` maps to IPv6; `CNAME` aliases one name to another name (not an IP directly); `MX` specifies mail servers; `TXT` holds arbitrary text, commonly used for domain ownership verification. DNS changes don't take effect everywhere instantly -- PROPAGATION is the delay caused by caches at every layer holding onto an old answer until their TTL (time-to-live) expires.
topics.analogy: DNS is a phone book (and its caching layers are photocopies of pages you've already looked up): instead of memorizing the actual phone number (IP address) for everyone you call, you look up a name and get the current number back -- and if that number changes, anyone still holding an old photocopy (a cached record) keeps dialing the old number until their copy is due for a refresh (TTL expiry).

examples.code: nslookup github.com
examples.note: Actually run: returned a real, current IP address for github.com from a live DNS query -- a genuine name-to-address resolution, not a simulated one. Output includes the resolving server used and the resolved address.

mistakes: Changing a DNS record and expecting it to take effect everywhere instantly -- caches at your OS, router, ISP, and other resolvers around the world will keep serving the OLD answer until their TTL expires, which can take minutes to (rarely) days depending on the record's configured TTL.

Confusing a CNAME (aliases to another NAME) with an A record (maps directly to an IP) -- a CNAME can't coexist with other records on the exact same name because of how alias resolution works, a common real misconfiguration.
Assuming a failed DNS lookup means the target server is down -- it only means the NAME couldn't be resolved to an address; the server itself may be perfectly healthy and reachable directly by IP.
topics.handsOn: Run `nslookup` (or `dig` on Linux/macOS) against a real domain you use often and note the returned IP address(es). Then look up what TTL value a DNS record you control (or a public one) is configured with, and explain what that number means in practical terms.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what DNS does in one sentence, name at least 3 record types and what each is for, and explain why DNS changes don't propagate instantly.

checks.q: You just changed your domain's A record to point to a new server, but some visitors are still hitting the old server 20 minutes later. Why?
checks.a: DNS answers are cached at multiple layers (the visitor's OS, their router, their ISP's resolver) for as long as the record's TTL (time-to-live) specifies. Anyone whose cache hasn't expired yet will keep resolving to the old IP until their cached copy's TTL runs out -- this is normal DNS propagation delay, not a sign the change failed.

keyTakeaways: DNS translates domain names into IP addresses via a chain of servers, with heavy caching at every layer for speed.
A/AAAA records map to IP addresses; CNAME aliases to another name; MX specifies mail servers; TXT holds arbitrary verification/config text.
DNS changes propagate gradually, gated by each cache layer's TTL -- not instantly.

topics.title: curl and debugging network requests
topics.concept: `curl` is the standard command-line tool for making HTTP(S) requests directly, without a browser -- essential for debugging APIs, testing servers, and scripting network interactions. Key flags: `-s` (silent, suppress progress output), `-I` (HEAD request, headers only, no body), `-X METHOD` (choose GET/POST/PUT/DELETE/etc.), `-H "Header: value"` (add a request header), `-d 'data'` (send a request body, commonly with `-X POST`), `-w "format"` (print specific metrics like status code or timing after the request), `-v` (verbose -- shows the full request AND response, including headers, useful for seeing exactly what was sent). When something over the network breaks in production, curl is very often the very first tool reached for to isolate whether the problem is DNS, connectivity, the server's response, or something else entirely.
topics.analogy: curl is talking to a server directly in its own language instead of going through a translator (a browser's UI) -- you see exactly what was sent and exactly what came back, which is precisely what you need when debugging, rather than a browser's rendered, simplified view of the same exchange.

examples.code:
curl -sI https://api.github.com | head -5
echo '---'
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "Status: %{http_code} | DNS: %{time_namelookup}s | Connect: %{time_connect}s | Total: %{time_total}s\n" https://api.github.com
examples.note: Actually run against GitHub's real API: the -I flag shows real response headers (status line, Date, Cache-Control, etc.) without downloading a body; the -w format string breaks down the REAL timing of DNS lookup, TCP connect, and total request time as separate measured phases -- exactly how you'd isolate whether slowness is DNS, connection setup, or the server's own response time.

mistakes: Forgetting `-X POST` (or another method) and defaulting to GET when trying to hit a POST-only endpoint, then being confused by a 404/405 that's really just "wrong method", not "endpoint doesn't exist."
Not using `-s` in a script and having curl's progress bar/meter output pollute captured output that a script is trying to parse.

Debugging "the API doesn't work" by only checking the response body, when curl's timing breakdown (`-w` with `%{time_namelookup}`, `%{time_connect}`, etc.) can immediately show whether the real problem is DNS, connection, or slow server response.
topics.handsOn: Pick a real public API (e.g. `https://api.github.com`) and use curl to: (1) get just the response headers with `-I`, (2) get the full timing breakdown with a `-w` format string like the example above, (3) intentionally request a method or path that should fail, and observe the resulting status code.
topics.doneWhen: You can use curl to inspect headers, check a status code, and break down where time is spent in a request (DNS vs connect vs total).

checks.q: An API call is slow. How would curl's timing flags help you figure out WHERE the time is going?
checks.a: curl's -w format string can report time_namelookup (DNS resolution time), time_connect (TCP connection setup time), and time_total (the whole request) as separate numbers -- comparing them tells you whether the slowness is DNS resolution, establishing the connection, or the server itself taking a long time to respond, rather than guessing.

keyTakeaways: curl makes direct HTTP(S) requests from the command line -- essential for debugging APIs without a browser in the way.
-I (headers only), -X (method), -H (headers), -d (body), and -w (custom output/timing) are the flags you'll use constantly.
curl's timing breakdown can isolate whether slowness is DNS, connection setup, or the server's own response time.

topics.title: Firewalls and security groups
topics.concept: A FIREWALL controls what network traffic is allowed in or out of a machine or network, based on rules matching things like source IP, destination port, and protocol -- everything not explicitly allowed is typically denied by default (a 'default-deny' posture, the safer default). In cloud environments, this concept is usually implemented as a SECURITY GROUP (AWS) or equivalent (Azure Network Security Group, GCP Firewall Rules): a virtual firewall attached to a VM or resource, with INBOUND rules (what's allowed to reach it) and OUTBOUND rules (what it's allowed to reach). A classic real misconfiguration is opening a database port (like 5432 or 3306) to `0.0.0.0/0` ("anywhere on the internet") instead of restricting it to only the specific application servers that legitimately need it -- the PRINCIPLE OF LEAST PRIVILEGE says every rule should allow only exactly what's needed, nothing broader.
topics.analogy: A security group is a building's guest list checked at the door, not a general "is anyone allowed to knock" policy -- by default no one gets in, and each rule is a specific, named exception ("the delivery service is allowed in through the loading dock, no one else"). Opening a database port to the entire internet is like removing that guest list entirely for one specific door -- convenient in the moment, and a real, common cause of production data breaches.

examples.code:
# Conceptual security group rules (AWS-style), not a live infrastructure change:
# INBOUND rules for a web server:
#   allow  tcp  port 443  from  0.0.0.0/0        (public HTTPS traffic -- intentionally open)
#   allow  tcp  port 22   from  203.0.113.0/24    (SSH only from a known office/VPN IP range)
# INBOUND rules for that web server's DATABASE (a separate machine/security group):
#   allow  tcp  port 5432 from  <web-server-security-group-only>   (NOT 0.0.0.0/0)
#   deny   everything else, by default
examples.note: Doc-grounded, not executed in this environment (no real cloud account/security-group infrastructure to configure here) -- this exact structure (default-deny, explicit narrow allow rules, database traffic restricted to only the application tier that needs it) matches AWS's own documented security group best practices.

mistakes: Opening a database or admin port to `0.0.0.0/0` "temporarily" to debug something, and forgetting to close it afterward -- this is one of the single most common real causes of cloud data breaches.

Writing one overly broad rule ("allow all traffic between these two security groups") instead of narrow, specific rules per port/protocol -- broad rules make it much harder to reason about what's actually allowed later.

Confusing a firewall/security group (which controls network REACHABILITY) with authentication (which controls who's allowed to log in once they can reach the service) -- both matter, and one being correct doesn't make the other unnecessary.
topics.handsOn: Sketch out (on paper or in notes) the inbound security-group rules you'd want for a typical two-tier app: a public web server and a private database it talks to. Be specific about which ports are open to the whole internet versus only to the other tier.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain the default-deny principle, distinguish inbound from outbound rules, and identify why opening a database port to 0.0.0.0/0 is a real security risk.

checks.q: Why is opening a database's port to 0.0.0.0/0 ("anywhere") considered a serious security misconfiguration, even if the database itself requires a password?
checks.a: It means literally anyone on the internet can attempt to connect to that database, turning password strength into your ONLY line of defense -- brute-force attempts, credential leaks, or a future vulnerability in the database software all become directly exploitable from anywhere. Restricting the port to only the specific application servers that need it removes that entire attack surface regardless of password strength.

keyTakeaways: Firewalls/security groups control allowed network traffic by rule, defaulting to deny-everything-not-explicitly-allowed.
Cloud security groups have separate inbound (what can reach a resource) and outbound (what it can reach) rules.
Principle of least privilege: every rule should be as narrow as possible -- opening sensitive ports to the whole internet is a common, serious real-world mistake.

topics.title: Load balancers and reverse proxies
topics.concept: A REVERSE PROXY sits in front of one or more backend servers and forwards incoming requests to them -- clients only ever talk to the proxy, never directly to the backend. A LOAD BALANCER is a reverse proxy specifically distributing incoming requests ACROSS MULTIPLE backend instances, so no single server gets overwhelmed and traffic keeps flowing even if one instance goes down. Common distribution strategies: ROUND ROBIN (requests cycle evenly across instances), LEAST CONNECTIONS (send the next request to whichever instance currently has the fewest active connections), and IP HASH (the same client IP consistently routes to the same backend, useful when a session needs to stick to one instance). A HEALTH CHECK is the load balancer periodically pinging each backend instance and automatically routing traffic away from any instance that stops responding correctly -- this is what makes horizontal scaling and zero-downtime deployments practically possible.
topics.analogy: A load balancer is a host at a restaurant's entrance directing each new party to whichever table/server currently has the least going on, rather than everyone crowding the first waiter they see -- and if one waiter (server instance) goes on an unplanned break, the host simply stops sending new parties their way until they're back, without the restaurant ever fully stopping service.

examples.note: Doc-grounded, not executed here (no running nginx/backend cluster in this authoring environment) -- this configuration syntax and the `least_conn` load-balancing directive match nginx's own official documentation exactly. `proxy_pass` is what makes nginx forward incoming traffic to whichever backend the `upstream` block selects, rather than serving the request itself.

mistakes: Assuming a load balancer alone makes an application highly available -- if the application itself can't handle concurrent instances correctly (e.g. storing session state only in one instance's local memory instead of a shared store), load balancing just spreads the same bugs across more machines.

Not configuring (or ignoring) health checks -- without them, a load balancer keeps sending traffic to a crashed or unresponsive instance, turning what should be an invisible failure into a real, user-facing one.

Confusing a reverse proxy (server-side, forwards to backends the client never sees directly) with a forward proxy (client-side, forwards a client's outgoing requests, e.g. for anonymity or corporate filtering) -- they solve very different problems despite the similar name.
topics.handsOn: Sketch a small architecture diagram: a load balancer in front of 3 backend instances, with a health check periodically probing each one. Describe in your own words what happens to traffic if one instance fails its health check.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what a reverse proxy and a load balancer each do, name at least two load-balancing strategies, and explain why health checks matter.

checks.q: One of three backend instances behind a load balancer crashes. What should happen to user-facing traffic, and what mechanism makes that happen?
checks.a: Traffic should continue flowing normally to the other two healthy instances with no visible outage to users. This works because the load balancer's health checks detect the crashed instance stops responding correctly, and it automatically stops routing new requests to it until it recovers.

keyTakeaways: A reverse proxy sits in front of backend servers and forwards requests to them; a load balancer is a reverse proxy that also distributes traffic across multiple backend instances.
Round robin, least connections, and IP hash are common distribution strategies, each suited to different needs.
Health checks let a load balancer automatically route around a failed instance -- the mechanism that makes horizontal scaling and zero-downtime deploys actually work.

title: Git & Version Control for Operations
why: The Common Core already covered basic Git (init/add/commit/push) -- this module goes deeper into what operations/DevOps work specifically needs: branching strategies for teams, actually resolving a merge conflict instead of just avoiding one, keeping secrets out of your repo, automating checks with hooks, and using Git as the literal source of truth for infrastructure state (GitOps), which later modules on CI/CD and Kubernetes build directly on top of.

topics.title: Branching strategies for teams
topics.concept: A BRANCH is an independent line of development -- multiple people (or automated pipelines) can work in parallel without stepping on each other's changes until they explicitly merge. TRUNK-BASED DEVELOPMENT keeps one long-lived branch (`main`/`trunk`) that everyone merges into frequently (often daily), using very short-lived feature branches (hours to a couple of days) -- favored by teams wanting fast, continuous integration and deployment. GIT FLOW uses several long-lived branches with defined roles (`main` for releases, `develop` for integration, `feature/*` for individual features, `release/*` and `hotfix/*` for stabilizing a release) -- more structured, but slower-moving and harder to keep in sync, which is why most modern CI/CD-driven teams have shifted toward trunk-based development or a lighter variant of it.
topics.analogy: Trunk-based development is a small team all editing the same shared document with frequent, small saves -- conflicts stay small and get caught immediately. Git Flow is multiple teams each keeping their own draft for weeks before a big, formal merge into the master copy -- more ceremony, and the longer a branch lives separately from `main`, the more it and `main` have drifted, making the eventual merge bigger and riskier.

examples.code:
git checkout -b feature/add-health-check
# ... make changes, commit ...
git push -u origin feature/add-health-check
# open a pull/merge request into main
# once approved and merged, delete the branch:
git branch -d feature/add-health-check
examples.note: This is the real, standard trunk-based/short-lived-feature-branch workflow: branch off main, do focused work, merge back quickly via a reviewed pull request, then delete the branch -- verified against GitHub's and GitLab's own documented recommended flow.

mistakes: Letting a feature branch live for weeks without merging -- the longer it diverges from `main`, the more likely a large, painful merge conflict becomes later.

Choosing Git Flow's full ceremony (develop/release/hotfix branches) for a small team shipping continuously -- it adds real process overhead that mostly pays off for teams doing scheduled, versioned releases (e.g. shipping numbered software releases), not continuous deployment.
Committing directly to `main` without a branch/pull-request for anything beyond a trivial fix -- this skips code review and CI checks that a branch-based workflow gives you almost for free.
topics.handsOn: Create a new branch, make a small change, commit it, and (if you have a remote) push it and open a pull request. Then delete the local branch after merging, and explain in your own words when you'd reach for Git Flow instead of trunk-based development.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain the core difference between trunk-based development and Git Flow, and you've created, used, and cleaned up a feature branch.

checks.q: Why do most modern CI/CD-driven teams favor trunk-based development over Git Flow's longer-lived branches?
checks.a: Short-lived branches that merge into main frequently keep divergence small, so conflicts stay small and get caught quickly -- which pairs naturally with continuous integration/deployment. Git Flow's longer-lived develop/release/hotfix branches add real process overhead and let branches drift further from main before merging, which mostly pays off for teams doing scheduled, versioned releases rather than continuous deployment.

keyTakeaways: Branches let parallel work happen without conflicting until an explicit merge.
Trunk-based development: one long-lived main branch, short-lived feature branches, frequent merges -- favored for continuous deployment.
Git Flow: multiple long-lived branches with defined roles -- more structured, better suited to scheduled/versioned releases.
