topics.title: Merging and resolving a real conflict
topics.concept: `git merge branch-name` combines another branch's changes into your current branch. Most merges are AUTOMATIC -- Git can tell the changes don't overlap. A CONFLICT happens when the same lines were changed differently on both branches, and Git can't decide which version is correct -- it stops and marks the conflicting section directly in the file with `<<<<<<< HEAD` (your current branch's version), `=======` (a separator), and `>>>>>>> branch-name` (the incoming branch's version). Resolving a conflict means manually editing the file to keep the correct content, DELETING the conflict markers themselves, then `git add`-ing the resolved file and committing to complete the merge. `git merge --abort` cancels an in-progress conflicted merge entirely, returning you to exactly where you were before attempting it -- useful when you realize you need more context before resolving properly.
topics.analogy: A merge conflict is two people editing the same paragraph of a shared document differently at the same time -- the document (Git) can't guess which version you meant to keep, so it shows you BOTH versions side by side and waits for a human to decide, rather than silently picking one and hoping it's right.

examples.code:
git checkout -b feature/new-thing
echo 'v2-feature' > app.txt && git add app.txt && git commit -m 'feature work'
git checkout main
echo 'v2-main' > app.txt && git add app.txt && git commit -m 'main work'
git merge feature/new-thing
cat app.txt
examples.note: Actually run: this exact sequence produced a genuine merge conflict (Git reported 'CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in app.txt'), and cat'ing the file afterward showed real conflict markers: <<<<<<< HEAD / v2-main / ======= / v2-feature / >>>>>>> feature/new-thing -- not a simulated example, a real conflicted merge state.

mistakes: Committing a "resolved" file that still contains the `<<<<<<<`/`=======`/`>>>>>>>` marker lines -- this is a genuine, common mistake that breaks the file's actual content; always search for these markers before committing a resolution.
Panicking and force-pushing over the conflict instead of resolving it -- `git merge --abort` safely returns you to the pre-merge state if you need to step back and reassess.
Resolving a conflict by blindly keeping "your" version (HEAD) without reading what the incoming branch actually changed -- this can silently discard real, needed work from the other branch.
topics.handsOn: Reproduce the example above yourself: create two branches that edit the same line of the same file differently, merge one into the other, and manually resolve the resulting conflict by editing out the markers and choosing (or combining) the correct content.
topics.doneWhen: You've caused and manually resolved a real merge conflict, including removing the conflict markers and completing the merge with a commit.

checks.q: After resolving a merge conflict by editing the file, what two steps are still required to actually complete the merge?
checks.a: You must `git add` the resolved file(s) to mark the conflict as resolved, then run `git commit` to complete the merge with a merge commit -- editing the file alone doesn't finish the merge process.

keyTakeaways: A conflict happens when the same lines changed differently on both branches -- Git marks it directly in the file with <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> markers.
Resolving means editing the file to the correct content, removing the markers entirely, then `git add` + `git commit`.
`git merge --abort` safely cancels an in-progress conflicted merge if you need to step back.

handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If you commit and later notice literal `<<<<<<<` text still in the file, you left a marker in during resolution — this is a genuinely common real mistake, always search the file for these markers before committing.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `git add <file>` then `git commit` (no `-m` needed — Git pre-fills a merge commit message).
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: A successful merge commit — check the file's final content one more time to confirm it's exactly what you intended, not an accidental half-resolution.

topics.title: .gitignore and keeping secrets out of version control
topics.concept: A `.gitignore` file tells Git which files/patterns to never track (build artifacts, dependency folders, local logs, and critically, files containing secrets like `.env`) -- entries can be exact filenames, patterns (`*.log`), or whole directories (`node_modules/`). Once a file is genuinely untracked, `.gitignore` prevents it from ever being accidentally staged with a broad `git add -A`. But `.gitignore` only prevents FUTURE tracking -- if a secret was ALREADY committed at some point in history, adding it to `.gitignore` afterward does nothing to remove it from existing commits; it remains in the repository's history and (if ever pushed) potentially in every clone/fork, requiring history-rewriting tools (like `git filter-repo`) and, for real leaked credentials, ROTATING the actual secret (issuing a new one and revoking the old), not just deleting the file.
topics.analogy: .gitignore is telling a filing clerk in advance never to file certain categories of document into the permanent record. But if a document was already filed and duplicated into several archives before you gave that instruction, telling the clerk to stop filing new copies does nothing to retrieve the ones already out there -- the only real fix at that point is invalidating whatever the leaked document authorized (rotating the secret), not just removing the file going forward.

examples.code:
echo '*.log' > .gitignore
echo '.env' >> .gitignore
touch debug.log
echo 'API_KEY=secret123' > .env
git add -A
git status --short
examples.note: Actually run: after adding *.log and .env to .gitignore, a broad `git add -A` staged ONLY .gitignore itself -- debug.log and .env, despite existing on disk, never appeared as staged files, confirming .gitignore genuinely prevents them from being tracked.

mistakes: Adding a secret file to .gitignore AFTER it was already committed once, and assuming that removes it from history -- it doesn't; the secret remains in every existing commit and must be treated as compromised (rotate it) plus removed from history separately if needed.

Committing a real `.env` file "just this once for convenience" -- there is no safe "just this once" with secrets in version control; treat every commit as potentially permanent and world-readable the moment it's pushed.

Forgetting that `.gitignore` patterns are relative to where the file lives (or the repo root, for a top-level one) -- a pattern that looks right can silently fail to match files in a different directory than expected.
topics.handsOn: Create a .gitignore with entries for a log file pattern and a secrets file, create matching files on disk, then run `git add -A` and confirm via `git status` that the ignored files never get staged.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what .gitignore does and does NOT protect against, and why rotating a leaked secret matters even after removing the file.

checks.q: You just discovered an API key was accidentally committed to a public repo 3 commits ago, and you've since added the file to .gitignore. Is the secret safe now?
checks.a: No. .gitignore only prevents FUTURE tracking -- the secret still exists in the repository's history in that earlier commit, and if the repo was ever pushed publicly, it may already be cloned/cached elsewhere. The correct fix is to immediately rotate the actual secret (issue a new one, revoke the old), and separately consider rewriting history to remove it if needed -- simply adding it to .gitignore now does not undo the earlier exposure.

keyTakeaways: .gitignore prevents matching files from being tracked/staged going forward -- exact names, patterns, or whole directories.
It does nothing to remove a secret that was already committed in an earlier commit -- that requires history rewriting AND rotating the actual secret.
Treat any committed-and-pushed secret as compromised immediately -- rotation, not just deletion, is the real fix.

resources.label: GitHub Docs — Removing sensitive data from a repository

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `echo '*.log' > .gitignore` then `echo '.env' >> .gitignore`.
Create matching files: `touch debug.log` and `echo 'API_KEY=secret123' > .env`.
Run `git add -A` then `git status --short`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Only `.gitignore` itself shows as staged (e.g. `A  .gitignore`) — `debug.log` and `.env` exist on disk but never appear, even with the broad `-A` flag.
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If a file you expected to be ignored still shows up staged, check that your .gitignore pattern's path is relative to the right place — a pattern that looks correct can silently not match a file in a different directory than you assumed.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write one sentence: if `.env` had already been committed once BEFORE you added it to .gitignore, would adding it now remove it from history?
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: No — .gitignore only prevents FUTURE tracking; anything already committed remains in history and must be treated as compromised (rotate the secret), regardless of gitignore changes made afterward.

topics.title: Git hooks and pre-commit checks
topics.concept: A Git HOOK is a script Git automatically runs at specific points in its workflow (before a commit, before a push, after a merge, etc.) -- stored as executable files in `.git/hooks/`, named after the event they respond to (`pre-commit`, `pre-push`, `post-merge`). A `pre-commit` hook runs right before a commit is finalized; if it exits with a NONZERO status code, Git aborts the commit entirely -- the standard mechanism for automatically blocking bad commits (secrets, failing linters, broken formatting) before they ever enter history, rather than relying on developers remembering to check manually every time. Hooks are LOCAL by default (they live in `.git/hooks/`, which isn't tracked/shared via a normal clone) -- tools like `pre-commit` (the framework) or `husky` (for Node projects) solve this by letting a hook's actual CONFIGURATION be committed to the repo and installed automatically for every contributor.
topics.analogy: A pre-commit hook is a security guard checking a package before it's allowed to leave the building -- if the guard finds something disallowed, the package is turned back at the door, before it ever gets shipped anywhere. Because the raw hook script itself doesn't travel with the repo by default, teams use a shared configuration (checked into the repo) so every new team member's checkout gets the same guard automatically, rather than each person having to remember to hire their own.

examples.code:
cat > .git/hooks/pre-commit << 'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
if git diff --cached --name-only | grep -q '\.env$'; then
  echo "ERROR: refusing to commit .env file"
  exit 1
fi
EOF
chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit
git add -f .env
git commit -m "oops trying to commit secrets"
examples.note: Actually run: this real pre-commit hook checks the list of STAGED files for anything named .env, and when a genuinely staged .env file was committed against, the hook printed its error message and the commit was GENUINELY BLOCKED (nonzero exit code) -- confirmed no commit was created for that attempt.

mistakes: Writing a hook that doesn't `exit 1` (or any nonzero code) on failure -- a hook that only prints a warning but exits 0 doesn't actually block anything; Git only cares about the exit code, not the printed output.

Relying purely on a raw `.git/hooks/` script for a team, forgetting it isn't shared by a normal `git clone` -- every new team member's hook is empty until you adopt a framework (pre-commit, husky) that installs shared, version-controlled configuration automatically.

Making a pre-commit hook too slow (e.g. running a full test suite on every commit) -- this trains developers to reach for `--no-verify` to skip it out of frustration, defeating its purpose; keep pre-commit checks fast, save slower checks for CI.
topics.handsOn: Write a real pre-commit hook (like the example above) that blocks committing a specific filename or pattern, make it executable, and confirm both that it blocks a matching commit AND that an unrelated commit still succeeds normally.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what a Git hook is, write a working pre-commit hook that blocks a commit, and explain why hooks aren't shared by default via a normal clone.

checks.q: Your pre-commit hook script runs and prints an error message, but the commit still goes through anyway. What's the most likely bug in the hook?
checks.a: The hook script isn't actually exiting with a nonzero status code on the failure path. Git only blocks the commit if the hook's exit code is nonzero -- printing an error message alone has no effect if the script still returns exit code 0.

keyTakeaways: Git hooks are scripts Git runs automatically at specific workflow points (pre-commit, pre-push, etc.), stored in .git/hooks/.
A pre-commit hook that exits nonzero blocks the commit entirely -- the standard way to automatically catch secrets/lint failures/broken formatting before they enter history.
Raw hooks aren't shared via a normal clone -- frameworks like pre-commit or husky commit shared configuration so every contributor gets the same checks automatically.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Create `.git/hooks/pre-commit` containing a bash script that checks `git diff --cached --name-only` for anything matching `.env`, printing an error and `exit 1` if found.
Run `chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit` to make it executable.
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If your hook doesn't run at all, double-check it's executable (`chmod +x`) and named exactly `pre-commit` with no file extension — Git looks for that exact filename.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Force-stage a real `.env` file (`git add -f .env`) and try `git commit -m "oops"`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Your hook's error message printed, the commit REFUSED (nonzero exit code, no new commit created) — confirmed by running `git log --oneline -1` and seeing your previous commit still on top, not this one.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Unstage `.env`, then commit an unrelated file normally.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: This commit succeeds normally — the hook only blocks what it's specifically checking for, everything else passes through untouched.

topics.title: Tags, releases, and semantic versioning
topics.concept: A TAG is a permanent, named pointer to one specific commit -- unlike a branch, a tag doesn't move as new commits are added, making it the standard way to mark exactly what code shipped in a given release. An ANNOTATED tag (`git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "message"`) stores a tagger, date, and message, and is the recommended type for real releases; a LIGHTWEIGHT tag (`git tag v1.0.0`) is just a bare pointer with no extra metadata. SEMANTIC VERSIONING (semver) gives version numbers real meaning in the format `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`: increment MAJOR for breaking/incompatible changes, MINOR for new backward-compatible functionality, and PATCH for backward-compatible bug fixes -- so consumers of your software can tell from the version number alone whether upgrading is safe (patch/minor) or requires checking for breaking changes (major).
topics.analogy: A tag is a labeled photograph of the code at one exact moment -- unlike a branch (a living, moving conversation), the photograph never changes no matter what happens afterward. Semantic versioning is a nutrition label's serving-size convention: a consumer can read "2.3.1" and immediately know whether this is a routine refill (patch), a new-but-compatible ingredient (minor), or a genuinely different recipe that might disagree with them (major) -- without having to read every changelog line by line.

examples.code:
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First stable release"
git tag
git show v1.0.0 --stat
examples.note: Actually run: created a real annotated tag pointing at the current commit, listed it with `git tag`, and `git show` confirmed its metadata (tagger, date, message) is genuinely stored -- exactly the behavior an annotated tag is documented to have, versus a lightweight tag which stores none of that.

mistakes: Using a lightweight tag for a real release when you'll want to know later who tagged it and why -- annotated tags store that metadata, lightweight tags don't.

Bumping only the PATCH version after making a genuinely breaking change (e.g. removing a public function) -- this silently breaks anyone who upgrades expecting semver's promise that patch/minor releases are always safe.
Forgetting that tags, unlike branches, don't automatically get pushed to a remote — `git push` alone doesn't push tags; you need `git push --tags` (or `git push origin tag-name`) explicitly.
topics.handsOn: Create an annotated tag on your current commit with a real message, list all tags, and inspect the tag's metadata with `git show`. Then think through a hypothetical change to a project you know and decide whether it would warrant a major, minor, or patch version bump.
topics.doneWhen: You can create an annotated tag, explain the difference between annotated and lightweight tags, and correctly classify a change as major/minor/patch under semantic versioning.

checks.q: You add a new, optional parameter to a public function without changing any existing behavior. Under semantic versioning, should this be a major, minor, or patch bump?
checks.a: Minor. It's new functionality that's backward-compatible -- existing callers who don't use the new parameter are unaffected. Major is reserved for breaking/incompatible changes; patch is reserved for backward-compatible bug fixes, not new functionality.

keyTakeaways: A tag is a permanent pointer to one specific commit, marking exactly what shipped -- unlike a branch, it doesn't move.
Annotated tags store tagger/date/message metadata and are the recommended choice for real releases; lightweight tags are bare pointers.
Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) tells consumers from the version number alone whether an upgrade is safe or might break them.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First stable release"` on your current commit.
Run `git tag`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `v1.0.0` listed — a permanent pointer to this exact commit.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `git show v1.0.0 --stat`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Real metadata: `Tagger:`, `Date:`, and your message `First stable release` — this is specifically what an ANNOTATED tag stores that a lightweight tag (`git tag v1.0.0` with no `-a`/`-m`) would not.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Think of a real change to a project you know (or imagine one): adding a new optional parameter with a default value. Would that be a major, minor, or patch semver bump?
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Minor — it's a new capability that doesn't break existing callers (they don't have to pass the new parameter). A major bump would be for something that breaks existing usage; a patch would be for a bug fix with no behavior change.

topics.title: GitOps: git as the source of truth for infrastructure
topics.concept: GITOPS applies Git's own workflow -- version-controlled, reviewed, auditable changes -- not just to application code, but to INFRASTRUCTURE configuration itself (Kubernetes manifests, Terraform files, deployment configs). Instead of an engineer manually running commands against a live server or cluster, the DESIRED STATE of the infrastructure is described declaratively in files committed to a Git repository, and an automated controller continuously reconciles the ACTUAL running state to match whatever's currently in that repository -- so the repo, not any one person's memory or a manually-run command, is the single source of truth for "what should be running right now." This means every infrastructure change goes through the same review/approval/audit trail as an application code change (a pull request), and rolling back is as simple as reverting a commit, since the controller will automatically reconcile the live system back to match.
topics.analogy: GitOps is like a restaurant kitchen where the only way a dish's recipe can change is by editing the official written recipe book (and having a colleague review the edit) -- the kitchen staff (the automated controller) then continuously cook according to whatever the book currently says, rather than a chef occasionally walking in and changing a dish by hand without updating the book. If a bad edit gets made, reverting the book entry automatically brings the kitchen's output back in line -- no one has to remember what the dish used to taste like and manually recreate it.

examples.code:
# Conceptual GitOps workflow (this module's later modules cover the actual tools -- Kubernetes, Terraform -- in depth):
# 1. An engineer edits a Kubernetes deployment manifest file in a Git repo (e.g. bumping replicas: 3 -> 5)
# 2. They open a pull request; a reviewer approves and merges it into main
# 3. A GitOps controller (e.g. Argo CD, Flux) detects the change in the repo
# 4. The controller automatically applies the change to the live cluster to match
# 5. If the change causes a problem, reverting the merge commit causes the controller
#    to automatically reconcile the cluster back to the previous known-good state
examples.note: Doc-grounded, not executed in this environment (no live GitOps controller/cluster available here) -- this exact reconcile-from-Git workflow matches the official documentation for both Argo CD and Flux, the two most widely adopted GitOps controllers for Kubernetes.

mistakes: Manually running `kubectl apply` (or an equivalent direct change) against a live cluster that's supposed to be GitOps-managed -- the controller will detect the drift from what's in Git and may revert your manual change automatically, undoing it without warning.

Treating GitOps as only relevant to Kubernetes -- the same core idea (declarative desired state, version-controlled, automatically reconciled) applies just as well to Terraform-managed cloud infrastructure or configuration management generally.

Storing secrets in plaintext directly in the GitOps repository just because "it's all in Git anyway" -- the same secrets-in-version-control risk from earlier in this module applies; real GitOps setups use a secrets-management integration (e.g. sealed secrets, an external secrets operator) rather than plaintext values in the repo.
topics.handsOn: Sketch (on paper or in notes) what a GitOps-managed change would look like for scaling a service from 3 to 5 replicas: what file changes, what review step happens, and what automatically applies the change to the live system. Compare this to how you'd do the same scaling change manually, and identify what audit trail GitOps gives you that the manual approach doesn't.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what GitOps means, why Git becomes the single source of truth for infrastructure state, and what happens if someone manually changes a GitOps-managed system out-of-band.

checks.q: In a GitOps-managed Kubernetes cluster, an engineer manually runs kubectl to scale a deployment up during an incident, without updating the Git repository. What happens next, and why?
checks.a: The GitOps controller will detect that the live cluster's state has drifted from what's declared in the Git repository, and will typically reconcile the cluster back to match the repository -- effectively undoing the manual change, since Git (not the live cluster) is the source of truth. The correct fix during an incident is still to update the repository (even urgently, via a fast-tracked pull request), not to bypass it.

keyTakeaways: GitOps applies version control, review, and audit trails to infrastructure configuration, not just application code.
Desired state lives in Git; an automated controller continuously reconciles the live system to match it -- Git is the single source of truth.
Manual out-of-band changes to a GitOps-managed system risk being automatically reverted, since the controller enforces what's in the repo, not what's currently running.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Sketch the GitOps flow for scaling a service from 3 to 5 replicas: what FILE changes, what REVIEW step happens, and what automatically applies it to the live system.
Write out the same scaling change done manually instead (e.g. directly running a scale command against the live system) — no file change, no review, no automatic record.
Compare the two: write one sentence naming the specific audit-trail question GitOps can answer that the manual approach can't (e.g. 'who approved this exact change, and when').
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Something like: with GitOps, the pull request IS the audit trail — who proposed it, who approved it, and exactly what changed, permanently in Git history. The manual change leaves no equivalent record unless someone remembers to write one down separately.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write one more sentence: if someone ran a manual `kubectl apply` against a cluster that's supposed to be GitOps-managed, what would the GitOps controller eventually do?
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: It would detect the drift between the live cluster and what's declared in Git, and reconcile the cluster BACK to match Git — potentially undoing the manual change automatically, without warning, which is exactly why manual changes to a GitOps-managed system are a real mistake to avoid.

title: Containers & Docker
why: Containers are the standard unit of deployment across almost all modern infrastructure -- every module ahead (CI/CD, Kubernetes, cloud deployment) assumes you can build, run, and reason about a container. This module builds that foundation: why containers exist, writing a real Dockerfile, running and networking containers, and the practices that separate a toy container from a production-ready one.

topics.title: Why containers (and how they differ from VMs)
topics.concept: A CONTAINER packages an application together with everything it needs to run (code, runtime, libraries, config) into one portable unit -- but unlike a VIRTUAL MACHINE, containers share the HOST machine's operating system kernel rather than each running a full separate OS. This makes containers dramatically lighter (megabytes vs. gigabytes) and faster to start (fractions of a second vs. tens of seconds to minutes for a VM), at the cost of slightly weaker isolation than a full VM (since they share a kernel). The core promise containers solve is "it works on my machine" -- because a container image bundles the EXACT runtime environment the app was built against, it behaves identically on a developer's laptop, a CI pipeline, and a production server, since it's genuinely the same environment, not just similar.
topics.analogy: A VM is like giving each tenant their own entire building, plumbing and electrical system included -- maximally isolated, but slow to construct and resource-heavy. A container is like giving each tenant their own furnished apartment within one shared building (sharing the building's foundation and utilities, i.e. the host kernel) -- much faster to set up and far more space-efficient, with slightly less isolation between tenants than fully separate buildings would give.

examples.code:
# Conceptual comparison, not executed here (no running Docker daemon in this environment):
# Starting a VM:   often 30s-2min (boots a full separate kernel + OS)
# Starting a container: typically under 1 second (reuses the host's already-running kernel)
# Image size for a minimal web app:
#   VM image:        multiple GB (full OS + app)
#   Container image: tens to a few hundred MB (just app + its direct dependencies)
examples.note: Doc-grounded approximate figures matching Docker's and general virtualization documentation's own characterization of the tradeoff -- exact numbers vary by workload, but the order-of-magnitude difference (containers starting in under a second vs. VMs taking tens of seconds or more) is a well-documented, consistent property of the architecture difference, not a marketing claim.

mistakes: Assuming a container gives the exact same isolation guarantees as a VM -- containers share the host kernel, so a kernel-level vulnerability can, in some cases, affect all containers on that host; VMs have a stronger isolation boundary (a full separate kernel each).

Treating "it works in the container" as automatically meaning "it will work everywhere" without also considering environment-specific config (secrets, external service URLs) that legitimately differs between dev/staging/production even when the container image itself is identical.

Confusing a container IMAGE (the packaged, static blueprint) with a container (a running INSTANCE of that image) -- one image can be used to start many running containers, the same way one class can produce many objects.
topics.handsOn: Write down, in your own words, why a company running thousands of microservices would prefer containers over VMs for most of their workloads, and name one situation where a VM's stronger isolation might still be worth the extra overhead.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain the core architectural difference between a container and a VM, and articulate what problem containers solve ("works on my machine").

checks.q: What is the core architectural difference that makes containers lighter and faster to start than VMs?
checks.a: Containers share the host machine's operating system kernel, while each VM runs its own full, separate kernel/OS. Sharing the kernel means a container doesn't need to boot an entire OS to start, making it dramatically smaller and faster -- at the cost of slightly weaker isolation than a fully separate VM.

keyTakeaways: Containers package an app with its dependencies but share the host's kernel; VMs each run a full separate OS.
This makes containers much lighter and faster to start, at the cost of somewhat weaker isolation than a VM.
Containers solve "it works on my machine" by making the runtime environment genuinely identical everywhere, not just similar.

handsOnSteps.instruction: With Docker running on your machine, time how long `docker run --rm alpine echo hello` takes after the image is already pulled once.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Well under a second for the container itself to start and run — it's reusing your host's already-running kernel, not booting a separate OS.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write one sentence comparing that to how long a full VM typically takes to boot (tens of seconds to a couple minutes) — same rough order-of-magnitude gap Docker's own docs describe.
Write down one real situation where you'd still want a VM's stronger isolation despite the extra overhead (hint: running genuinely untrusted, potentially hostile code).
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Something like: multi-tenant hosting of code you don't trust at all — containers share the host kernel, so a kernel-level exploit can potentially affect sibling containers; a VM's separate kernel is a real, stronger boundary for that specific threat model.

topics.title: Writing your first Dockerfile
topics.concept: A DOCKERFILE is a text file of instructions describing how to build a container image. Key instructions: `FROM` picks a BASE IMAGE to build on top of (e.g. `node:20-slim`); `WORKDIR` sets the working directory inside the image for subsequent instructions; `COPY` copies files from your machine into the image; `RUN` executes a command DURING the build (e.g. installing dependencies) and its result is baked into the image; `EXPOSE` documents which port the container listens on (informational, doesn't actually publish it); `CMD` specifies the default command to run when a container STARTS (as opposed to `RUN`, which happens at build time). Each instruction creates a new LAYER, and Docker caches layers -- if an earlier instruction and its inputs haven't changed, Docker reuses the cached layer instead of re-running it, which is why instruction ORDER matters for build speed (put things that change rarely, like dependency installation, before things that change often, like your application code).
topics.analogy: A Dockerfile is a recipe card with steps executed in order, where each finished step's result gets photographed and reused next time if nothing about that step changed (layer caching) -- which is exactly why you put "buy and prep the rarely-changing pantry staples" before "chop today's specific vegetables": if only the vegetables changed, you can skip re-shopping for staples and start straight from that cached step.

examples.code:
FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --production
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
examples.note: Doc-grounded, not executed in this authoring environment (Docker Desktop is installed here but its daemon was not running, so no real container could be built/started while writing this lesson) -- this exact syntax and behavior is verified against Docker's own official documentation. Running it yourself on a machine with Docker running is the real, required verification step. This exact instruction ORDER (copying package.json and running npm ci BEFORE copying the rest of the source code) is Docker's own documented best practice specifically for layer-cache efficiency: application source code changes on nearly every commit, but dependencies change rarely -- so putting the dependency install before the broader COPY means most builds reuse the cached npm ci layer entirely.

mistakes: Copying the entire project (`COPY . .`) before running `npm install`/`npm ci` -- this means ANY source code change invalidates the dependency-install layer's cache, forcing a full reinstall on every single build even when dependencies didn't change.
Using `CMD` for something that should happen at build time (like installing packages) -- `CMD` only runs when a container STARTS, not during the image build; use `RUN` for build-time steps.

Forgetting `EXPOSE` doesn't actually publish a port to the host machine -- it's documentation for humans and some tooling; the real port mapping happens with `docker run -p host:container`, covered in the next lesson.
topics.handsOn: Write a Dockerfile for a simple app in a language you know, following the dependency-install-before-source-copy pattern shown above. Identify which of your instructions would be cached on a rebuild if you only changed one line of application code.
topics.doneWhen: You can write a basic Dockerfile with FROM/WORKDIR/COPY/RUN/EXPOSE/CMD and explain why instruction order affects build cache efficiency.

checks.q: Why does copying package.json and installing dependencies BEFORE copying the rest of your source code speed up repeated builds?
checks.a: Docker caches each instruction's layer and reuses it if nothing about that step changed. Since application source code changes far more often than dependencies, putting the dependency-install step first means most rebuilds (which only change source code) can reuse the cached dependency-install layer entirely, instead of reinstalling dependencies every single time.

keyTakeaways: A Dockerfile's core instructions: FROM (base image), WORKDIR, COPY, RUN (build-time), EXPOSE (documentation), CMD (container start command).
Each instruction is a cached layer -- instruction order matters for build speed, since a changed instruction invalidates its own cache and every layer after it.
Put rarely-changing steps (dependency installation) before frequently-changing ones (copying source code) to maximize cache reuse.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write a Dockerfile for a simple app you know, following this order: `FROM` a base image, `WORKDIR`, then COPY only the dependency manifest (e.g. `package.json`) and RUN the install, THEN `COPY . .` for the rest of the source.
With Docker running, build it twice in a row with no code changes: `docker build -t myapp:1.0 .` then again.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: The second build shows `CACHED` next to most steps and finishes almost instantly — nothing changed, so Docker reused every layer.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Change one line in your application source code (not the dependency file) and build a third time.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: The dependency-install `RUN` step still shows `CACHED`, but the `COPY . .` step and everything after it re-runs — exactly the point of putting the dependency install first: source changes (frequent) don't invalidate the expensive install step (rare to change).
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If EVERY step reruns even for a tiny source change, double check your Dockerfile copies the dependency manifest and runs the install BEFORE the broader `COPY . .` — the order is what makes caching work here, not just having separate steps.

topics.title: Building and running images
topics.concept: `docker build -t name:tag .` builds an image from a Dockerfile in the current directory (`.`), tagging it with a name and version. `docker run image-name` starts a new CONTAINER (a running instance) from that image. `docker run -p 8080:3000 image-name` maps port 3000 INSIDE the container to port 8080 on the HOST machine -- without this mapping, the container's port is not reachable from outside it, even if the app inside is listening correctly. `-d` runs the container detached (in the background, returning your terminal immediately); `docker ps` lists running containers; `docker logs container-id` shows a container's stdout/stderr output; `docker stop container-id` stops it; `docker exec -it container-id bash` opens an interactive shell INSIDE a running container -- essential for debugging what's actually happening inside.
topics.analogy: An image is a sealed blueprint/mold; `docker run` is casting an actual object from that mold -- you can cast many identical objects (containers) from the same mold (image). Port mapping (`-p 8080:3000`) is like connecting an internal intercom line (port 3000, inside the building) to an external phone number (port 8080) that the outside world can actually dial -- without that connection, the intercom works fine internally but nobody outside can reach it.

examples.code:
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
docker run -d -p 8080:3000 --name myapp-container myapp:1.0
docker ps
docker logs myapp-container
docker exec -it myapp-container bash
docker stop myapp-container

This exact command sequence (build with a tag, run detached with a port mapping and a name, inspect with ps/logs, get an interactive shell, then stop) matches Docker's own official CLI reference documentation for each command's flags and behavior.

mistakes: Running a container without `-p` and then being confused why the app "isn't reachable" from the host machine -- the app inside may be running perfectly; without an explicit port mapping, nothing outside the container can reach it.

Forgetting `-d` for a long-running service and having it block your terminal in the foreground (or accidentally killing it with Ctrl+C when you meant to detach) -- use `-d` for anything meant to keep running.

Debugging a failing container purely by staring at `docker ps`'s summary output instead of checking `docker logs` (for what the app itself printed) or `docker exec -it ... bash` (to poke around inside it directly) -- these are the two most useful real debugging tools for a misbehaving container.

checks.q: You ran a container and its app is definitely running (confirmed via logs), but you can't reach it from your browser. What's the most likely missing piece?
checks.a: A port mapping (-p host:container) was likely never specified, or maps the wrong ports. Without an explicit -p flag, a container's internal port isn't exposed to the host machine at all, even though the app inside is running and listening correctly.

keyTakeaways: docker build creates an image from a Dockerfile; docker run starts a container (a running instance) from that image.
-p host:container maps a container's internal port to a reachable port on the host -- without it, the app isn't reachable from outside.
docker logs and docker exec -it ... bash are the two core tools for debugging what's actually happening inside a running container.

topics.title: Docker networking and volumes
topics.concept: By default, each Docker container gets its own isolated network namespace -- containers can't reach each other unless explicitly connected. Creating a USER-DEFINED NETWORK (`docker network create mynet`) and running multiple containers on it (`docker run --network mynet ...`) lets them reach each other BY CONTAINER NAME (Docker provides automatic DNS resolution within a shared network) -- e.g. an app container can reach a database container simply by hostname `db`, no IP address needed. Container filesystems are EPHEMERAL by default -- anything written inside a container is lost when that container is removed. A VOLUME (`docker run -v myvolume:/data ...`) persists data outside the container's own lifecycle, on the host, surviving container removal/recreation -- essential for anything stateful, like a database's actual data files.
topics.analogy: Docker's default per-container network isolation is like every apartment having its own private phone line with no shared directory -- a user-defined network is installing a shared building directory where any apartment can just dial another by name ("ring unit 'db'") instead of needing to know its exact private number. A volume is a storage unit OUTSIDE any individual apartment -- when a tenant (container) moves out and a new one moves in, whatever's in the external storage unit is still there, untouched, unlike anything left inside the apartment itself.

examples.code:
docker network create app-network
docker run -d --name db --network app-network -v db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16
docker run -d --name api --network app-network -e DATABASE_HOST=db myapi:1.0

Running it yourself on a machine with Docker running is the real, required verification step. This pattern (shared user-defined network + named volume for the stateful service) matches Docker's own official networking and storage documentation. The api container can reach the db container simply via the hostname 'db' (set as DATABASE_HOST) because both share the app-network -- no hardcoded IP address needed, and Docker's built-in DNS resolves 'db' to that container automatically.

mistakes: Running two containers that need to talk to each other with no shared network, then trying to reach one via `localhost` from inside the other -- from inside a container, `localhost` refers to that container itself, not the host machine or a sibling container.

Storing a database's actual data files only inside the container's own filesystem (no volume) -- removing or recreating that container (e.g. during a routine update) silently destroys all its data, since container filesystems are ephemeral by default.

Hardcoding another container's IP address instead of using its container name over a shared network -- container IPs can change on restart; names resolved via Docker's built-in DNS are the stable, correct approach.

checks.q: Two containers, api and db, are both running but api can't reach db at all. What's the most likely cause?
checks.a: They're most likely not on the same Docker network. By default, each container gets its own isolated network namespace; containers can only reach each other by name if they're explicitly placed on a shared user-defined network.

keyTakeaways: Containers are network-isolated by default -- a shared user-defined network lets them reach each other by container name via Docker's built-in DNS.
Container filesystems are ephemeral -- data written inside a container is lost when it's removed unless it's stored in a volume.
Volumes persist data outside a container's own lifecycle, essential for anything stateful like a database.

handsOnSteps.instruction: With Docker running, create a network: `docker network create app-network`.
Run two simple containers on it, e.g. `docker run -d --name one --network app-network alpine sleep 300` and `docker run -d --name two --network app-network alpine sleep 300`.
Run `docker exec one ping -c 2 two`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: 2 successful ping replies — container `one` reached container `two` BY NAME, because Docker's built-in DNS resolves container names to their current IP automatically on a shared user-defined network.
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If ping fails with 'unknown host', double check both containers are on the SAME network (`docker network create` + `--network app-network` on both `docker run` commands) — containers on different (or no) networks genuinely can't reach each other by name.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Create a named volume and write a file into it via one container: `docker volume create demo-data` then `docker run --rm -v demo-data:/data alpine sh -c "echo hello > /data/test.txt"`.
Run a completely NEW container mounting that same volume: `docker run --rm -v demo-data:/data alpine cat /data/test.txt`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `hello` printed — the file persisted in the named volume even though the container that wrote it is already gone (`--rm` removed it), proving the data lives in the volume, not in any one container.

topics.title: Docker Compose for multi-container apps
topics.concept: Real applications are rarely one container -- a typical setup might have an API, a database, and a cache, each in their own container. DOCKER COMPOSE lets you define an entire multi-container setup declaratively in one YAML file (`compose.yaml`), specifying each SERVICE's image (or build context), ports, environment variables, volumes, and dependencies -- then bring the whole stack up or down with a single command. `docker compose up` starts every defined service (building images if needed, creating a shared network automatically so services can reach each other by name); `docker compose down` stops and removes them; `docker compose up -d` runs it all detached; `depends_on` controls STARTUP ORDER (though notably, it does not wait for a dependency to be fully READY, just started -- a common source of "my app started before the database was actually accepting connections" bugs).
topics.analogy: Compose is a single seating chart and instruction sheet for an entire event with multiple staff roles (services), instead of separately, manually telling each staff member where to stand and what to do one at a time -- one document describes the whole event's setup, and one command ("places, everyone") gets every role into position together.

examples.code:
# compose.yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:3000"
    environment:
      - DATABASE_HOST=db
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpassword
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
volumes:
  db-data:

This YAML structure (services/build/ports/environment/depends_on/volumes, plus a top-level named volume declaration) matches Docker Compose's own official file reference exactly. Compose automatically creates a shared network for all services in this file, so 'api' can reach 'db' by that hostname with no manual network setup required (unlike the previous lesson's manual docker network create step).

mistakes: Assuming `depends_on` guarantees the dependency is fully ready (e.g. the database has finished initializing and is accepting connections) -- it only guarantees the dependency's container has STARTED, not that it's ready; apps that connect immediately on startup often need their own retry logic for this reason.

Committing real secrets (like the example's plaintext POSTGRES_PASSWORD) directly into a compose file meant for a real environment -- fine for local development, but production setups should pull secrets from a secrets manager or environment-specific `.env` file that's itself gitignored.
Forgetting `docker compose down -v` removes named volumes too (deleting persisted data) — plain `docker compose down` alone stops/removes containers and networks but preserves volumes by default.

checks.q: Your app service has depends_on pointing at your database service, but the app still crashes on startup trying to connect to the database. Why might depends_on alone not be enough?
checks.a: depends_on only guarantees the dependency's CONTAINER has started, not that the service inside it is actually ready to accept connections (e.g. a database still initializing). The app needs its own retry/backoff logic when connecting on startup, since a started container isn't the same as a ready one.

keyTakeaways: Docker Compose defines a multi-container application declaratively in one YAML file, managed as a single unit with docker compose up/down.
Compose automatically creates a shared network so services can reach each other by name, with no manual network setup.
depends_on controls startup order but not readiness -- apps still need their own connection retry logic for dependencies that take time to become ready.

handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: It resolves and connects — Compose automatically creates a shared network for every service in the file, so `db` is reachable by name with zero manual `docker network create` step, unlike the previous lesson's manual setup.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run `docker compose down`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Containers and the network are removed, but the named volume (if any) survives — confirm with `docker volume ls`.
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If your data unexpectedly disappeared, check whether you ran `docker compose down -v` instead of plain `down` — the `-v` flag additionally removes named volumes, deleting persisted data along with the containers.

topics.title: Image best practices: multi-stage builds and running as non-root
topics.concept: A MULTI-STAGE BUILD uses multiple `FROM` instructions in one Dockerfile, where an early stage does the heavy lifting (compiling code, installing build-only dependencies) and a later, final stage copies ONLY the finished artifact from the earlier stage into a much smaller base image -- discarding all the build-time tooling and intermediate files from the final image entirely. This produces dramatically smaller, more secure production images (less installed software means a smaller attack surface). Separately, Docker containers run as the ROOT user by default unless told otherwise -- meaning a compromised process inside the container runs with root privileges INSIDE that container's namespace, which is a real, avoidable risk; adding a `USER` instruction to switch to a non-root user before the final `CMD` is a widely-recommended security practice, since it limits what a compromised process can actually do even if it does execute code.
topics.analogy: A multi-stage build is like a workshop that builds furniture (the build stage, full of saws/glue/sawdust/scrap material) but only ships the finished chair itself to the customer (the final stage) -- the customer's living room (your production image) never has to house the entire workshop's mess just because the chair was built there. Running as non-root is giving a delivery worker a key that only opens the specific room they need, rather than a master key to the whole building -- if that specific key is ever stolen, the damage is contained to one room instead of everything.

examples.code:
# Multi-stage build with a non-root final user:
FROM node:20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
RUN useradd --system --uid 1001 appuser
USER appuser
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

Running it yourself on a machine with Docker running is the real, required verification step. This exact pattern -- a build stage building the app, a separate final stage copying only the compiled output via COPY --from=build, and a dedicated non-root USER for the final runtime -- matches Docker's own documented best practices for both multi-stage builds and running containers securely.

mistakes: Copying the entire build stage's directory (including devDependencies, source TypeScript files, build caches) into the final image instead of just the compiled output -- this defeats the purpose of a multi-stage build; be deliberate about exactly which files `COPY --from=build` pulls forward.

Adding `USER appuser` but then finding the app crashes because it needs write access to a directory only root can write to -- switching to non-root sometimes requires explicitly granting that user permission to specific directories the app genuinely needs to write into (e.g. a cache or upload folder).

Assuming a smaller image is automatically a more secure one without also checking WHAT's still installed -- multi-stage builds reduce size and surface area, but a final image can still include unnecessary packages if the final base image or COPY step brings more along than intended.
topics.handsOn: Rewrite a Dockerfile you've already written (or the earlier example) as a multi-stage build, and add a dedicated non-root USER before the final CMD. Compare (conceptually, or by actually building both if you have Docker running) the final image's size against a single-stage equivalent.
topics.doneWhen: You can write a multi-stage Dockerfile that ships only the finished artifact, and you can explain why running as a non-root user reduces real security risk.

checks.q: Why does a multi-stage Dockerfile typically produce a smaller and more secure final image than a single-stage build?
checks.a: The build stage can install heavy build-only tooling (compilers, dev dependencies) freely, since none of that is carried into the final image -- only the specific compiled artifact is copied forward via COPY --from=build into a fresh, minimal base image. This means the final image ships less installed software overall, reducing both its size and its attack surface.

keyTakeaways: A multi-stage build uses multiple FROM instructions -- an early stage does the heavy build work, a final stage copies only the finished artifact into a minimal image.
Containers run as root by default unless a USER instruction switches to a non-root user, which limits what a compromised process inside the container can actually do.
Smaller, non-root final images are widely recommended production practices, not just optimizations -- they genuinely reduce real attack surface.

topics.title: Container registries: sharing images
topics.concept: A CONTAINER REGISTRY stores and distributes container images -- Docker Hub is the largest public registry (the default source for `FROM` base images like `node`, `python`, `postgres`), and every major cloud provider offers its own private registry (Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure Container Registry) for storing an organization's own images securely. An image's full name has the form `[registry/]repository:tag` -- omitting the registry defaults to Docker Hub, and omitting the tag defaults to `latest` (which is just a convention/label, NOT guaranteed to always mean "newest" -- it's whatever image was most recently pushed without an explicit tag, which is why production deployments should always pin an EXPLICIT version tag, never rely on `latest`). `docker push registry/repo:tag` uploads a locally-built image; `docker pull registry/repo:tag` downloads one -- this is exactly how a CI/CD pipeline (next module) gets a built image onto a production server: build once, push to a registry, then pull that exact same image wherever it needs to run.
topics.analogy: A container registry is a library's shelving and catalog system: Docker Hub is the big public library anyone can browse and borrow from, while a private cloud registry is an organization's own restricted-access archive. Tagging an image is like a book's specific edition number -- relying on "latest" is like asking a librarian for "whatever edition is currently on the shelf," which could quietly change to a different edition tomorrow; citing an exact edition number (an explicit version tag) is the only way to guarantee you and a colleague are looking at the identical thing.

examples.code:
docker tag myapp:1.0 myregistry.example.com/team/myapp:1.0
docker push myregistry.example.com/team/myapp:1.0
# ...later, on a different machine or server...
docker pull myregistry.example.com/team/myapp:1.0
docker run -d myregistry.example.com/team/myapp:1.0
examples.note: Doc-grounded, not executed in this authoring environment (Docker Desktop is installed here but its daemon was not running, so no real container could be built/started while writing this lesson) -- this exact syntax and behavior is verified against Docker's own official documentation. Running it yourself on a machine with Docker running is the real, required verification step. This exact tag-then-push-then-pull workflow (with an EXPLICIT version tag, not `latest`) matches Docker's own official documentation for distributing images via a registry, and is precisely the mechanism a CI/CD pipeline relies on to get one specific, verifiable build artifact from where it's built to wherever it needs to run.

mistakes: Deploying production services tagged only `latest` -- since `latest` just means "whatever was pushed most recently without an explicit tag," this makes it impossible to know exactly which build is running, and a redeploy can silently pull in an unintended newer image; always pin an explicit version tag in production.

Storing private/proprietary application images on a fully public registry without checking its visibility settings -- a repository can accidentally be public by default on some registries, exposing your application's code and dependencies.

Forgetting that `docker pull` (and a container's own `FROM` instruction) fetches from Docker Hub by default if no registry is specified -- confusing this with your organization's own private registry can lead to pulling the wrong (public) image entirely if a name collides.

checks.q: Why is deploying a production service with only the `latest` tag considered risky, even though it seems convenient?
checks.a: `latest` is just a label meaning "whatever image was most recently pushed without an explicit tag" -- it is not guaranteed to always mean the newest or most stable version, and it can change silently. This makes it impossible to know exactly which build is actually running, and a redeploy can pull in an unintended, different image. Production deployments should always pin an explicit version tag instead.

keyTakeaways: A container registry stores and distributes images -- Docker Hub is the largest public one; cloud providers offer private ones for an organization's own images.
An image name is [registry/]repository:tag -- omitting the registry defaults to Docker Hub, omitting the tag defaults to `latest`.
`latest` is just a convention, not a guarantee of newest/stable -- production deployments should always pin an explicit version tag.

title: CI/CD & Automation
why: Manually building, testing, and deploying software doesn't scale past a handful of changes -- CI/CD automates that entire cycle so every change is verified and shipped the same reliable way, every time, without a human remembering every step. This module covers the concepts and a real, runnable workflow example, building directly on this path's Git and Docker modules.

topics.title: What CI/CD actually means
topics.concept: CONTINUOUS INTEGRATION (CI) means automatically building and testing every code change (usually on every push or pull request) so integration problems are caught immediately, in small increments, rather than discovered later when many changes have piled up together. CONTINUOUS DELIVERY means every change that passes CI is automatically prepared into a releasable state (built, tested, packaged) but a human still explicitly triggers the actual production deployment. CONTINUOUS DEPLOYMENT goes one step further: every change that passes all automated checks is deployed to production automatically, with no manual approval step at all. The core value across all three: automation replaces error-prone manual steps with the exact same repeatable process every single time, and catching problems early (in a small, recent change) is dramatically cheaper to fix than catching them late (after many changes have piled on top).
topics.analogy: Manually testing and deploying software is like a chef tasting and re-plating every dish from scratch by hand, at a different quality level depending on how tired they are that day. CI/CD is having a standardized, automated line that checks and prepares every single dish identically, every time, regardless of how the day's going -- consistency and catching a problem is about the process, not about anyone remembering every step correctly under pressure.

examples.code:
# Conceptual spectrum, not code to run:
# CI only:                  every push is built + tested automatically, deploy is fully manual
# Continuous Delivery:      every push that passes CI is packaged and READY to deploy, a human clicks "deploy"
# Continuous Deployment:    every push that passes CI is deployed to production automatically, no human step at all
examples.note: Conceptual illustration of the three terms' real distinction, matching how they're consistently defined across CI/CD tooling documentation (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI) -- the difference is entirely about WHERE the human approval gate sits, not how thorough the automated checks are.

mistakes: Using "CI/CD" as one interchangeable term when the distinction matters -- a team doing Continuous Deployment (no manual gate at all) has a very different risk profile and testing-rigor requirement than one doing Continuous Delivery (a human still approves the actual release).
Believing CI/CD means "no humans involved" -- even Continuous Deployment still involves humans; they just act on failures/alerts rather than manually approving every single successful change.

Adopting Continuous Deployment before genuinely trusting your automated test suite -- skipping the human gate only makes sense once your automated checks are actually catching the problems that would have needed a human to notice.
topics.handsOn: For a project you know (personal or otherwise), decide which of the three levels (CI only / Continuous Delivery / Continuous Deployment) it currently operates at, and explain what would need to be true about its test suite before it could safely move to Continuous Deployment.
topics.doneWhen: You can clearly distinguish Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery, and Continuous Deployment, and explain why catching problems early is cheaper than catching them late.

checks.q: What is the key practical difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
checks.a: Continuous Delivery automatically prepares every passing change into a releasable state, but a human still explicitly triggers the actual production deployment. Continuous Deployment removes that manual gate entirely -- every change that passes automated checks deploys to production with no human approval step.

keyTakeaways: CI automatically builds and tests every change; CD (in either form) extends that toward automatically shipping it.
Continuous Delivery keeps a human approval gate before production deploy; Continuous Deployment removes it entirely.
Automation's value is consistency and catching problems early, when they're small and cheap to fix, not just "fewer humans involved."

topics.title: Anatomy of a pipeline
topics.concept: A PIPELINE is the automated sequence of STAGES a code change passes through -- typically BUILD (compile/package the code), TEST (run automated tests), and DEPLOY (ship it somewhere). Pipelines are FAIL-FAST by convention: if any stage fails, later stages don't run at all -- there's no point deploying code that failed its tests. Stages can run SEQUENTIALLY (each waits for the previous to finish) or, where independent, IN PARALLEL (e.g. running unit tests and a linter simultaneously, since neither depends on the other's result) to reduce total pipeline time. Every pipeline run has an overall exit status derived directly from its stages' exit codes -- exactly the same exit-code convention you've already used with individual shell commands.
topics.analogy: A pipeline is an assembly line with mandatory quality checkpoints: if the quality-control station (the test stage) rejects a unit, it simply never proceeds to the shipping station (deploy) -- there's no override, by design, because shipping a failed unit defeats the entire point of having the checkpoint.

examples.code:
cat > pipeline.sh << 'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

echo "=== Stage 1: Build ==="
echo "Compiling application..."

echo "=== Stage 2: Test ==="
run_tests() {
  echo "Running test suite..."
  return 1   # simulating a failing test
}
if run_tests; then
  echo "Tests passed"
else
  echo "Tests FAILED -- aborting pipeline before deploy"
  exit 1
fi

echo "=== Stage 3: Deploy ==="
echo "Deploying to production..."
EOF
chmod +x pipeline.sh
./pipeline.sh
echo "Pipeline exit code: $?"
examples.note: Actually run: this real bash pipeline genuinely stopped after the (deliberately simulated) failing test stage and never printed the Deploy stage's output at all -- the pipeline's final exit code was 1, confirming fail-fast behavior is a real, mechanical consequence of exit codes and control flow, not just a policy someone has to remember to enforce.

mistakes: Writing a pipeline where a failing test's exit code gets accidentally swallowed (e.g. by piping its output through another command without checking `pipefail`) -- this can let a genuinely broken build silently proceed to deploy.
Running stages in parallel that actually have a hidden dependency (e.g. a test stage that needs the build stage's output) -- parallelizing only makes sense for genuinely independent stages.

Treating a pipeline's "green checkmark" as proof the software definitely works correctly -- it only proves the specific checks that were run passed; a pipeline is only as good as the tests and checks it actually contains.
topics.handsOn: Run the pipeline.sh example above and confirm the Deploy stage's output never prints when the test stage fails. Then modify `run_tests` to return 0 (success) instead, rerun, and confirm the Deploy stage now does print.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain the build/test/deploy stage structure, why fail-fast matters, and when parallel stages make sense versus sequential ones.

checks.q: Why do CI/CD pipelines conventionally stop entirely the moment any stage fails, rather than continuing on to later stages?
checks.a: Later stages (especially deploy) assume earlier stages succeeded -- deploying code that failed its own tests defeats the entire purpose of having automated tests in the first place. Fail-fast ensures a broken change never reaches production just because a later stage happened to still run.

keyTakeaways: A pipeline is a sequence of stages (typically build/test/deploy) that a change passes through automatically.
Fail-fast: any stage failing stops the pipeline, preventing later stages (especially deploy) from running on broken code.
Independent stages can run in parallel to reduce total pipeline time; dependent stages must run sequentially.

topics.title: Your first GitHub Actions workflow
topics.concept: GitHub Actions defines pipelines as YAML WORKFLOW files in `.github/workflows/`. A workflow has TRIGGERS (`on:`, e.g. `push`, `pull_request`) specifying when it runs, one or more JOBS (each running on a fresh virtual machine, specified via `runs-on:`), and each job has a sequence of STEPS -- either `uses:` (running a reusable pre-built ACTION from GitHub's marketplace, like checking out code or setting up a language runtime) or `run:` (running a raw shell command directly). Jobs run in PARALLEL by default unless one explicitly declares `needs: other-job-name`, which makes it wait for that job to succeed first -- exactly the sequential-vs-parallel stage concept from the previous lesson, expressed in GitHub's specific syntax.
topics.analogy: A GitHub Actions workflow file is a checklist handed to a fresh temporary worker (a freshly-provisioned virtual machine) every single time: it lists exactly what to check out, what tools to install, and what commands to run, in order -- because the worker has zero memory of any previous run, the checklist must be completely self-contained every time.

examples.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build

  deploy:
    needs: build-and-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Deploying to production..."
examples.note: Doc-grounded, not executed against a real CI runner in this authoring environment (no GitHub Actions runner available here) -- this exact YAML structure and behavior is verified against GitHub Actions' own official documentation. The underlying fail-fast/stage-sequencing logic it describes was separately confirmed with a real, executed bash pipeline in this lesson's first example. This exact structure (triggers, runs-on, actions/checkout + actions/setup-node as the standard checkout/language-setup actions, needs: for job dependency, and an if: condition gating deploy to only the main branch) matches GitHub Actions' own official syntax and the actions/checkout and actions/setup-node actions' own published usage documentation.

mistakes: Forgetting `actions/checkout` as the first step -- without it, the runner's fresh virtual machine has no copy of your repository's code at all; every workflow that needs your code must explicitly check it out first.
Assuming jobs run in the order they're written in the file -- by default, ALL jobs in a workflow run in PARALLEL; you must explicitly add `needs:` to enforce an order/dependency between them.

Putting the `if:` condition gating a production deploy on the wrong job, or forgetting it entirely -- without it, a deploy job with no branch restriction could run for every pull request, not just merges to main.

checks.q: By default, do multiple jobs in one GitHub Actions workflow file run sequentially in the order they're written, or in parallel?
checks.a: In parallel, by default. Jobs only run sequentially/in a specific order if one explicitly declares `needs: other-job-name`, which makes it wait for that job to succeed before starting.

keyTakeaways: GitHub Actions workflows are YAML files in .github/workflows/, triggered by events like push/pull_request.
Jobs run on fresh VMs and run in parallel by default; needs: enforces a dependency/order between them.
Steps are either uses: (a reusable pre-built action) or run: (a raw shell command) -- actions/checkout is almost always the first step needed.

topics.title: Automated testing in a pipeline
topics.concept: A pipeline's TEST stage is only as valuable as the tests it actually runs -- CI doesn't invent test coverage, it just automatically enforces whatever tests already exist, on every single change. The TEST PYRAMID is a common way to think about test investment: many fast, cheap UNIT tests (testing one small piece of code in isolation) at the base, fewer INTEGRATION tests (testing multiple pieces working together, e.g. against a real database) in the middle, and a small number of slow, expensive END-TO-END tests (testing the whole system as a real user would) at the top -- because unit tests are fast and cheap to run on every single change, while end-to-end tests are slow and better reserved for a smaller, critical set of user flows. A pipeline should fail the build the moment any test fails, and TEST COVERAGE metrics (what percentage of code is exercised by tests) are a useful signal but not a goal in themselves -- 100% coverage with weak assertions catches far less than 70% coverage with genuinely meaningful tests.
topics.analogy: The test pyramid is like a building's structural inspection process: many quick, cheap checks on individual materials happen constantly (unit tests), fewer but more thorough checks on how sections fit together happen periodically (integration tests), and a full walkthrough of the finished building happens rarely, right before handover (end-to-end tests) -- you wouldn't do a full building walkthrough after every single nail is hammered, but you also wouldn't skip it entirely and only check individual nails.

examples.code:
# Conceptual test-pyramid distribution for a typical web app's CI suite:
# ~70% unit tests      -- fast (milliseconds each), test one function/component in isolation
# ~20% integration tests -- slower (seconds each), test a real API endpoint against a real test database
# ~10% end-to-end tests  -- slowest (can be minutes), test a full user flow through the real UI
examples.note: Conceptual illustration of the test pyramid's typical proportions, matching the widely-cited testing pyramid concept (originated by Mike Cohn) as documented across major testing frameworks' own guidance (e.g. Testing Library, Playwright docs both explicitly reference this same shape when recommending test strategy).

mistakes: Inverting the pyramid -- writing mostly slow end-to-end tests and few unit tests -- which makes the test suite slow to run and flaky (end-to-end tests are more prone to unrelated failures like timing issues), discouraging developers from running it often.
Chasing a coverage percentage as a goal rather than a signal -- code can have 100% line coverage while its tests never actually assert anything meaningful about correct behavior.

Not running the full test suite in CI for every single change, and instead relying on developers to "remember" to run tests locally before pushing -- the entire value of CI is that this happens automatically, every time, without relying on memory.
topics.handsOn: For a project you know (or a hypothetical one), sketch roughly how you'd distribute test effort across unit/integration/end-to-end tests, and identify one specific user flow important enough to deserve a slower end-to-end test.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain the test pyramid's shape and reasoning, and why coverage percentage alone isn't a reliable quality signal.

checks.q: Why does the test pyramid recommend having many unit tests but only a few end-to-end tests, rather than an even split?
checks.a: Unit tests are fast and cheap to run (milliseconds, isolated), so you can afford to run many of them on every single change. End-to-end tests are slow and more prone to unrelated flakiness (real UI timing, network calls), so having too many of them makes the whole suite slow and unreliable to run often -- reserving them for a smaller set of critical user flows keeps the suite both fast and trustworthy.

keyTakeaways: A pipeline's test stage automatically enforces whatever tests exist -- it doesn't create test coverage on its own.
The test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, a small number of slow end-to-end tests.
Coverage percentage is a signal, not a goal -- meaningful assertions matter more than raw coverage numbers.

handsOnSteps.instruction: For a project you know, write down roughly how many tests exist today (or would need to) at each level: unit, integration, end-to-end.
Compare your numbers to the typical pyramid shape (~70% unit / ~20% integration / ~10% end-to-end). Write one sentence: is your project pyramid-shaped, or inverted (more slow tests than fast ones)?
