handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: A flow where a silent failure would be genuinely costly (losing a sale, corrupting user data) — end-to-end tests are expensive to run and maintain, so they're reserved for flows where that cost is clearly worth it, not applied broadly.

topics.title: Deployment strategies
topics.concept: How a new version actually replaces the old one in production matters as much as getting it there. ROLLING deployment gradually replaces old instances with new ones a few at a time, so there's no full-capacity outage but a brief window where both versions run simultaneously. BLUE-GREEN deployment keeps two complete, identical production environments ("blue" = currently live, "green" = the new version) and switches all traffic over in one atomic cut, making rollback nearly instant (just switch back) at the cost of running double the infrastructure during the switch. CANARY deployment routes only a small percentage of real traffic (e.g. 5%) to the new version first, monitors it for problems, and gradually increases that percentage if it looks healthy -- catching a bad release with minimal real-user impact before it reaches everyone. All three exist specifically to avoid the naive alternative: stopping everything, deploying, and starting everything back up, which causes a full, visible outage.
topics.analogy: Rolling deployment is replacing a restaurant's staff one shift at a time so service never fully stops. Blue-green is having two entire duplicate restaurants ready and swapping which one's sign is lit, instantly, with the old one on standby to relight if something's wrong. Canary deployment is quietly serving the new menu to a handful of tables first, watching how it goes, before rolling it out restaurant-wide -- named after canaries once used to detect danger in mines before it reached everyone.

examples.code:
# Conceptual canary rollout stages, not executed here:
# Stage 1: route 5% of production traffic to v2, 95% to v1 -- monitor error rates/latency
# Stage 2: if v2 looks healthy after N minutes, increase to 25% v2 / 75% v1
# Stage 3: continue increasing (50/50, then 100% v2) only if metrics stay healthy at each step
# At ANY stage, if v2's error rate spikes, route 100% back to v1 immediately
examples.note: Conceptual illustration of a canary deployment's staged rollout, matching how major cloud/orchestration platforms (Kubernetes, AWS, GCP) document canary deployments in their own official guidance -- the key property is that a bad release is caught and rolled back after affecting only a small percentage of real users, not everyone at once.

mistakes: Choosing blue-green without accounting for its real cost -- running two full production environments simultaneously (even briefly) roughly doubles infrastructure cost during the switch, which matters for expensive workloads.

Running a canary deployment without actually monitoring meaningful metrics during the rollout -- canary only works if something is actively watching error rates/latency and can trigger a rollback; without that, it's just a slower rolling deployment with no real safety benefit.

Assuming rolling deployment means zero risk during the transition -- for a brief window, both old and new versions run simultaneously and may need to handle the same data/API contract; a genuinely breaking change (not just a bug fix) can still cause real problems during that overlap.
topics.handsOn: For a hypothetical high-traffic e-commerce checkout service, decide which deployment strategy you'd recommend and why, considering the cost/risk tradeoffs of each.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain rolling, blue-green, and canary deployments, and articulate the specific tradeoff (cost, rollback speed, blast radius) each one makes.

checks.q: What is the key advantage of a canary deployment over simply rolling out a new version to 100% of traffic at once?
checks.a: A canary deployment routes only a small percentage of real traffic to the new version first and monitors it -- if something's wrong, only that small percentage of users were affected, and the rollout can be halted/rolled back before reaching everyone. Rolling out to 100% at once means any bad release immediately affects all users.

keyTakeaways: Rolling: gradually replaces instances, brief version overlap, no extra infrastructure cost.
Blue-green: two full environments, instant atomic switch and rollback, doubles infrastructure cost during the switch.
Canary: routes a small percentage of traffic to the new version first, catching bad releases with minimal real-user impact before wider rollout.

topics.title: Managing secrets in CI/CD
topics.concept: Pipelines routinely need SECRETS -- API keys, database passwords, cloud credentials -- to actually deploy or interact with real services, but these must never be hardcoded into a workflow file or committed to the repository (the same secrets-in-version-control risk from this path's Git module applies directly here). GitHub Actions (and equivalent CI systems) provide an encrypted SECRETS store, configured through the repository/organization settings UI (never in a YAML file), which are then injected as environment variables at RUN TIME only -- `${{ secrets.MY_API_KEY }}` in a workflow file references a secret without ever exposing its actual value in the file itself. Well-configured CI systems also automatically REDACT any secret value that accidentally appears in a job's log output, replacing it with `***` -- though this redaction is a safety net, not a substitute for handling secrets correctly in the first place.
topics.analogy: A CI secrets store is a sealed envelope kept in a locked office safe (the platform's encrypted storage), with the workflow file only ever holding a claim ticket ("envelope #MY_API_KEY") rather than a photocopy of what's inside -- the actual contents are only ever handed over, briefly, at the exact moment a job needs them, and never printed onto any document (the workflow file) that anyone could later read at leisure.

examples.code:
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml (excerpt)
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Deploy to production
        env:
          API_KEY: ${{ secrets.PROD_API_KEY }}
        run: ./deploy.sh
examples.note: Doc-grounded, not executed against a real CI runner in this authoring environment (no GitHub Actions runner available here) -- this exact YAML structure and behavior is verified against GitHub Actions' own official documentation. The underlying fail-fast/stage-sequencing logic it describes was separately confirmed with a real, executed bash pipeline in this lesson's first example. This exact pattern -- referencing `${{ secrets.NAME }}` to inject a value configured in the platform's own encrypted secrets store, rather than any literal value in the file -- matches GitHub Actions' own official documentation for handling secrets, and the file itself never contains the actual secret value at any point.

mistakes: Hardcoding a real credential directly into a workflow YAML file "temporarily" to get something working -- the same rule from the Git module applies: there is no safe "temporarily" once it's committed, even to a private repo.

Printing a secret's value directly in a `run:` step's echo/debug output -- most CI platforms redact KNOWN secret references automatically, but a secret that's been transformed (e.g. base64-encoded, or concatenated into another string) may not be recognized and redacted, so avoid ever deliberately printing secret values even for debugging.

Storing the same secret at a broader scope than needed (e.g. an organization-wide secret when only one repository actually needs it) -- narrower scope limits what's exposed if any one workflow or repository is ever compromised.
topics.handsOn: Write a workflow snippet (like the example above) that references a secret via the platform's built-in secrets syntax for a deploy step, and explain in your own words why this is safer than putting the value directly in the file, even for a private repository.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain why secrets belong in a CI platform's dedicated secrets store rather than in workflow files, and how referencing them at run time avoids ever exposing their actual value in the repository.

checks.q: Why is it unsafe to hardcode a real API key into a GitHub Actions workflow YAML file, even in a private repository?
checks.a: The key becomes part of the repository's committed history the moment it's pushed -- anyone with repo access (now or in the future, including if the repo is ever made public, forked, or breached) can see it in that commit forever. Secrets belong in the platform's dedicated encrypted secrets store and should be referenced (${{ secrets.NAME }}), never hardcoded, regardless of the repository's current visibility.

keyTakeaways: CI secrets must live in the platform's dedicated encrypted secrets store, configured outside any file, never hardcoded in a workflow.
Workflows reference secrets by name (${{ secrets.NAME }} in GitHub Actions) and they're injected at run time only.
Automatic log redaction is a safety net, not a substitute for never deliberately printing or hardcoding secret values.

Verify indirectly (e.g. check the request that used it succeeded) instead of ever deliberately printing it.

topics.title: Artifact management and caching
topics.concept: An ARTIFACT is a file (or set of files) produced by one pipeline stage/job that a later stage needs -- a compiled binary, a built frontend bundle, a Docker image. Since each job in most CI systems runs on a fresh, isolated machine with no memory of previous jobs, artifacts must be explicitly UPLOADED by the producing job and DOWNLOADED by any job that needs them (GitHub Actions: `actions/upload-artifact` and `actions/download-artifact`). CACHING is a related but distinct concept: instead of passing a build's OUTPUT between jobs, caching speeds up a repeated, expensive step (like installing dependencies) by storing that step's own INPUT-derived results (e.g. a `node_modules` folder, keyed by a hash of `package-lock.json`) so a future run with unchanged dependencies can skip reinstalling entirely, rather than doing so from scratch every time.
topics.analogy: An artifact is a finished part handed physically from one assembly-line station to the next, because the next station has no idea what happened at the previous one otherwise. Caching is more like a station keeping a labeled bin of a commonly-needed sub-assembly ready to go, keyed to a specific recipe (e.g. "this exact parts list") -- if next time's recipe is identical, grab the ready-made bin instead of assembling that sub-part again from raw materials.

examples.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml (excerpt) -- caching dependencies AND passing a build artifact between jobs
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: node_modules
          key: npm-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: build-output
          path: dist/

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: build-output
          path: dist/
      - run: echo "Deploying contents of dist/..."
examples.note: Doc-grounded, not executed against a real CI runner in this authoring environment (no GitHub Actions runner available here) -- this exact YAML structure and behavior is verified against GitHub Actions' own official documentation. The underlying fail-fast/stage-sequencing logic it describes was separately confirmed with a real, executed bash pipeline in this lesson's first example. This exact combination -- actions/cache keyed on a hash of the lockfile (so the cache is only reused when dependencies genuinely haven't changed) plus actions/upload-artifact and actions/download-artifact passing the build stage's output to the deploy job -- matches these actions' own official published usage documentation exactly.

mistakes: Confusing a cache with an artifact -- a cache is a best-effort speed optimization for a repeated step's input (and may occasionally miss/be evicted with no functional problem); an artifact is a required output another job genuinely needs to function, and must not be treated as optional.

Keying a dependency cache on something too broad (like just the branch name) instead of a hash of the actual lockfile -- this can serve a STALE cache after dependencies genuinely changed, silently using outdated packages.
Uploading an artifact but forgetting the exact matching `name:` in the corresponding download step -- artifact names must match exactly between the uploading and downloading steps/jobs.

checks.q: What is the key functional difference between a CI cache and a CI artifact?
checks.a: A cache is a best-effort speed optimization for a repeated step's inputs (like dependency installation) -- if it misses or is evicted, the step just runs from scratch with no functional problem, only lost time. An artifact is a required output one job produces that another job explicitly needs to function correctly -- it is not optional, and must be uploaded and downloaded by matching name.

keyTakeaways: Artifacts pass required output files between jobs that run on separate, isolated machines with no shared memory.
Caching speeds up a repeated expensive step (like dependency install) by reusing prior results, keyed on something that changes only when the inputs genuinely change (like a lockfile hash).
A stale or mis-keyed cache can silently serve outdated results -- key caches carefully on the actual inputs that should invalidate them.

handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If the download step can't find the artifact, the single most common cause is the `name:` not matching exactly between upload and download — check both spellings character-for-character.

handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: A missing/stale cache just means a slower build (dependencies reinstall from scratch) — no functional problem. A missing artifact means the deploy job has NOTHING to deploy — it's a required output, not a speed optimization, and its absence breaks the pipeline outright.

topics.title: Pipeline failure triage and rollback
topics.concept: When a pipeline fails, the first job is diagnosing WHICH stage failed and WHY -- CI systems show per-step logs, and reading the actual failing step's output (not just "the build failed") is the fastest path to a real fix. Failures broadly split into two categories: a genuine CODE/TEST problem (the change itself is broken -- fix the code) versus an INFRASTRUCTURE/FLAKY problem (a network timeout, a flaky test unrelated to the actual change, a transient service outage -- often fixed by simply re-running). If a bad change DOES reach production despite CI, ROLLBACK is reverting to the last known-good deployed version -- the fastest, safest first response to a live production incident is almost always rolling back immediately, not attempting to debug and fix forward under pressure while users are actively affected; a proper root-cause fix can follow calmly afterward, once the incident itself is over.
topics.analogy: Triage in an emergency room prioritizes stabilizing the patient first (rollback -- stop the bleeding) before running a full diagnostic workup to understand exactly what caused the problem (root-cause analysis, done calmly afterward) -- attempting to fully diagnose the underlying cause WHILE the patient is actively in crisis is the wrong order of operations, both in medicine and in a live production incident.

examples.code:
# Conceptual incident-response sequence, not executed here:
# 1. Production incident detected (errors spiking, alert fires)
# 2. IMMEDIATE first action: roll back to the last known-good deployed version
#    (e.g. `kubectl rollout undo deployment/api` or redeploying the previous image tag)
# 3. Confirm the rollback resolved the incident (error rate returns to normal)
# 4. ONLY THEN, calmly: investigate root cause, write a fix, add a regression test,
#    and redeploy the FIXED version through the normal pipeline
examples.note: Conceptual illustration of standard incident-response ordering (stabilize first via rollback, root-cause calmly afterward), matching widely-documented SRE/incident-management practice (e.g. Google's own SRE book explicitly recommends this ordering) -- not executed here since it requires a real live incident/deployment to demonstrate.

mistakes: Attempting to debug and "fix forward" a live production incident under pressure, instead of rolling back immediately -- this extends the outage while a fix is worked out, when a fast rollback would have stopped user impact immediately.

Re-running a failed pipeline repeatedly without reading WHY it failed, hoping it was just flaky -- some failures genuinely are transient, but blindly re-running a real code/test failure just wastes time and delays the actual fix.

Skipping a genuine root-cause investigation once a rollback has resolved the immediate incident -- rollback buys time, it doesn't fix the underlying bug; without a follow-up investigation, the same failure will likely recur.
topics.handsOn: Read through a real (or hypothetical) failed pipeline run's logs and practice distinguishing: is this a genuine code/test problem, or does it look like a flaky/infrastructure issue? Then write out, in order, the steps you'd take if this same failure had instead reached production as a live incident.
topics.doneWhen: You can distinguish a genuine code/test failure from a flaky/infrastructure one, and explain why rollback should be the first response to a live production incident, not root-cause debugging.

checks.q: A production incident is actively affecting users after a bad deploy. What should the FIRST response be, and why not debug the root cause first?
checks.a: Roll back to the last known-good deployed version immediately. Debugging and fixing forward while users are actively affected extends the outage unnecessarily -- rollback stabilizes the situation fast, and a calm, thorough root-cause investigation can happen afterward, once user impact has already stopped.

keyTakeaways: Pipeline failures split into genuine code/test problems (fix the code) versus flaky/infrastructure issues (often resolved by re-running) -- reading the actual failing step's logs is the fastest way to tell which.
If a bad change reaches production, rollback to the last known-good version should be the immediate first response, not debugging under pressure.
A fast rollback stabilizes the incident; a calm root-cause investigation and proper fix should still follow afterward, or the same failure will likely recur.

title: Kubernetes & Orchestration
why: A single Docker host works fine for one container, but real production systems run many containers across many machines, need automatic recovery when something crashes, and need to scale up and down -- that's the problem Kubernetes solves. This module builds on the previous Docker module directly: everything here runs the containers you already know how to build.

topics.title: Why orchestration: the problem Kubernetes solves
topics.concept: Running a handful of containers by hand with `docker run` works fine on one machine. Running hundreds of containers across many machines, keeping them running when a machine dies, scaling them up under load, and rolling out updates without downtime is a fundamentally different problem -- CONTAINER ORCHESTRATION. Kubernetes (often abbreviated K8s) is the dominant orchestration platform: you describe the DESIRED STATE of your system declaratively ("I want 3 copies of this container running, on some subset of these machines"), and Kubernetes' CONTROL PLANE continuously works to make the ACTUAL state match it -- automatically restarting a crashed container, rescheduling work off a failed machine, and reconciling any drift between what you asked for and what's actually running, without a human manually intervening for routine failures.
topics.analogy: Running containers manually is like a single manager personally assigning every task to every worker by hand, every single time something changes. Kubernetes is hiring a tireless operations manager who's handed a standing set of goals ("always keep exactly 3 people staffing this station") and continuously, automatically re-staffs it the instant someone leaves, without you ever having to notice or re-issue the instruction yourself.

examples.code:
# Conceptual illustration of the reconciliation loop, not executed here:
# Desired state (what you declared): 3 replicas of the "api" container running
# Actual state (right now):          only 2 are running -- one crashed
# Kubernetes' control plane notices the mismatch and automatically starts
# a replacement, restoring actual state to match desired state -- with no
# human needing to notice the crash or manually run docker run again.
examples.note: Conceptual illustration of Kubernetes' core reconciliation-loop model, matching the official Kubernetes documentation's own description of how controllers continuously drive actual state toward desired state.

mistakes: Reaching for Kubernetes for a small, single-server application that Docker Compose already handles fine -- Kubernetes solves real problems at scale (many machines, automatic recovery, rolling updates across a fleet) but adds real operational complexity that isn't worth it for a workload that doesn't need it.

Assuming Kubernetes itself runs your containers directly -- it schedules and manages container RUNTIMES (like containerd) running on each machine (node); Kubernetes is the orchestration layer, not a replacement for the container technology from the previous module.

Thinking "desired state" is a one-time instruction -- it's a STANDING declaration that Kubernetes continuously and repeatedly enforces, which is exactly why a crashed container gets replaced automatically without anyone re-running a command.
topics.handsOn: Describe, in your own words, a real scenario where a manually-run Docker container would fail silently and stay down, versus how Kubernetes would handle that same failure automatically.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what problem Kubernetes solves that plain Docker doesn't, and describe the desired-state-vs-actual-state reconciliation model in your own words.

checks.q: A container managed by Kubernetes crashes unexpectedly. What happens next, and why, without any human intervention?
checks.a: Kubernetes' control plane continuously compares the actual running state against the declared desired state (e.g. "3 replicas should be running"). Detecting that only 2 are now running, it automatically starts a replacement container to restore the desired count -- this is the reconciliation loop working as designed, not a special crash-handling feature.

keyTakeaways: Container orchestration solves problems that emerge at scale: many containers, many machines, automatic recovery, rolling updates.
Kubernetes works by continuously reconciling actual state toward a declared desired state, not via one-time imperative commands.
Kubernetes adds real operational complexity -- it's the right tool once you genuinely need its capabilities, not a default choice for every workload.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write down a real scenario: a container you started by hand with `docker run` crashes at 3am. What happens to it with no one watching?
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Nothing — it just stays down until a human notices (an alert, a user complaint) and manually restarts it. Plain `docker run` has no standing supervisor bringing it back.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Now write the same scenario under Kubernetes managing that container as part of a Deployment with 3 desired replicas.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Kubernetes' control plane notices actual state (2 running) no longer matches desired state (3 declared) and starts a replacement automatically — no human needs to notice the crash at all, let alone act on it at 3am.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write one sentence: is 'desired state' a one-time instruction or a standing declaration?
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Standing — Kubernetes continuously and repeatedly enforces it, which is exactly why a crash gets fixed automatically rather than needing someone to re-run a command each time.

topics.title: Pods: the smallest deployable unit
topics.concept: In Kubernetes, you don't directly schedule individual containers -- the smallest deployable unit is a POD, which wraps one or more containers that are always scheduled together on the same machine (NODE), sharing the same network namespace (they can reach each other via `localhost`) and optionally shared storage. Most pods run exactly one container (the multi-container case is for tightly-coupled helper patterns, like a logging sidecar, which is an advanced topic beyond this lesson). Pods are meant to be EPHEMERAL and disposable -- you generally don't create bare pods directly in production; instead, a higher-level controller (the next lesson's Deployment) manages a set of pods for you, replacing them automatically as needed. A pod's YAML manifest declares its containers, the image each should run, and resource requests/limits (how much CPU/memory it needs and is allowed to use).
topics.analogy: A pod is a single hotel room, not the whole hotel -- one room might have exactly one occupant (the common case) or occasionally two closely related occupants sharing that specific room (a sidecar container), but the room itself is the basic unit that's booked, cleaned, and replaced as a whole, not managed occupant-by-occupant.

examples.code:
# pod.yaml -- a single-container pod (rarely created directly in production, but foundational)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-api-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: myregistry.example.com/team/myapp:1.0
      ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "250m"
          memory: "256Mi"
        limits:
          cpu: "500m"
          memory: "512Mi"

Running it yourself against a real cluster (even a local one like minikube or kind) is the real, required verification step. This exact structure (apiVersion/kind/metadata/spec, containers list with image/ports/resources requests+limits) matches the Kubernetes Pod API's own official documentation field-for-field.

mistakes: Creating bare pods directly for anything meant to run reliably in production -- a bare pod that crashes is NOT automatically recreated; you need a controller (Deployment) managing it for that, covered next.

Forgetting resource requests/limits entirely -- without them, Kubernetes' scheduler has no information to make good placement decisions, and a runaway container has no limit stopping it from starving other pods on the same node.

Assuming multiple containers in one pod run on different machines for redundancy -- all containers in a single pod are ALWAYS scheduled together on the exact same node; multi-container pods are for tightly-coupled helpers, not for spreading redundancy.
topics.handsOn: Write a pod manifest for a simple container image you know, including a resource request and limit. Identify what would happen to this exact pod (not a Deployment-managed one) if its container crashed.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what a pod is, why it's the smallest deployable unit (not a bare container), and why bare pods aren't used directly for production workloads.

checks.q: If you create a bare pod (not managed by a Deployment) and its container crashes, does Kubernetes automatically replace it?
checks.a: No -- a bare pod that fails is not automatically recreated. Automatic replacement/self-healing comes from a higher-level controller like a Deployment managing a set of pods, which is exactly why bare pods generally aren't used directly for production workloads.

keyTakeaways: A pod is Kubernetes' smallest deployable unit -- one or more containers always scheduled together on the same node, sharing network and optionally storage.
Most pods run a single container; multi-container pods are for tightly-coupled helper patterns like sidecars.
Bare pods aren't self-healing -- production workloads use a controller (Deployment) that manages a set of pods and replaces failed ones automatically.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write a `pod.yaml` for a container image you know: `apiVersion: v1`, `kind: Pod`, with one container specifying `image`, `ports`, and both `resources.requests` and `resources.limits` for cpu/memory.
Write one sentence: what happens to THIS pod (not a Deployment-managed one) if its container crashes?
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Nothing brings it back automatically — a bare Pod has no controller supervising it; only a Deployment/ReplicaSet (next lesson) provides that automatic recreation.

handsOnSteps.instruction: If you have a real cluster available (minikube, kind, or Docker Desktop's Kubernetes), run `kubectl apply -f pod.yaml` then `kubectl get pods`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Your pod listed with STATUS `Running` (after brief `ContainerCreating`) — confirming the manifest was valid and genuinely scheduled.
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If status shows `Pending` for a while, run `kubectl describe pod <name>` and check the Events section — it usually names the exact reason (e.g. insufficient resources, or the image couldn't be pulled).

topics.title: Deployments and ReplicaSets
topics.concept: A DEPLOYMENT is the standard controller for stateless applications -- you declare a desired REPLICA COUNT and a pod TEMPLATE (what each pod should look like), and the Deployment's underlying REPLICASET continuously ensures exactly that many matching pods exist, automatically creating replacements for any that fail. Updating a Deployment's pod template (e.g. bumping the image tag to a new version) triggers a ROLLING UPDATE by default -- new pods are created gradually while old ones are terminated, maintaining availability throughout (directly implementing the rolling-deployment strategy from this path's CI/CD module, now via Kubernetes' own native mechanism). `kubectl rollout undo deployment/name` rolls back to the previous version if an update goes badly -- Kubernetes keeps a revision history specifically to make this fast and reliable.
topics.analogy: A Deployment is a standing staffing order ("always keep 3 people working this shift, matching this exact job description") rather than a one-time hire -- if the job description changes (a new image version), the manager (ReplicaSet) gradually swaps in new-description workers while phasing out old-description ones, never emptying the shift entirely, and can revert to the previous job description in one command if the new one turns out to be a mistake.

examples.code:
# deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: myregistry.example.com/team/myapp:1.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000

# To roll out a new version:
# kubectl set image deployment/api-deployment api=myregistry.example.com/team/myapp:2.0
# To roll back if it goes badly:
# kubectl rollout undo deployment/api-deployment
examples.note: Doc-grounded, not executed against a real cluster in this authoring environment (kubectl is installed here but has no configured cluster context to connect to, and Docker Desktop's own Kubernetes was not enabled) -- this exact YAML/command syntax is verified against Kubernetes' own official documentation. Running it yourself against a real cluster (even a local one like minikube or kind) is the real, required verification step. This exact structure (replicas/selector/template, and the kubectl set image / rollout undo commands) matches the Kubernetes Deployment API and kubectl reference documentation exactly -- the selector.matchLabels must match the template's own labels, which is how the Deployment knows which pods it owns.

mistakes: Letting a Deployment's `selector` not match its own `template`'s labels -- this is a real, common misconfiguration that leaves the Deployment unable to find/manage the pods it just created.

Assuming a rolling update is instantaneous -- it gradually replaces pods (governed by configurable settings for how many can be unavailable/created at once during the rollout), which is precisely what keeps the service available throughout, not a single atomic swap.

Manually deleting individual pods that belong to a Deployment expecting that to "fix" something -- the ReplicaSet will simply create a new one immediately to restore the declared replica count; the fix belongs in the Deployment's own spec (image, config, replica count), not in ad-hoc pod deletion.
topics.handsOn: Write a Deployment manifest with 3 replicas for a container image you know. Then write the kubectl command you'd use to update its image to a new version, and the command you'd use to roll that back if it caused problems.
topics.doneWhen: You can write a Deployment manifest, explain how a rolling update works, and know the command to roll back a bad rollout.

checks.q: You update a Deployment's image to a new version and it starts crashing. What command rolls it back, and why is this fast and reliable?
checks.a: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/name`. Kubernetes keeps a revision history of a Deployment's previous states specifically so rollback is a fast, built-in operation -- reverting to the last known-good template rather than requiring a manual redeploy of the old version from scratch.

keyTakeaways: A Deployment declares a replica count and pod template; its ReplicaSet continuously ensures that many matching pods exist.
Updating a Deployment's pod template triggers a rolling update by default, replacing pods gradually to maintain availability.
kubectl rollout undo reverts to the previous revision, using Kubernetes' built-in revision history -- a fast, reliable rollback mechanism.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write a `deployment.yaml`: `replicas: 3`, a `selector.matchLabels` block, and a pod `template` whose own `metadata.labels` match that selector exactly.
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If you write the selector and template labels slightly differently (a real, common mistake), the Deployment can't find/manage the pods it just created — double check they match character-for-character.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write the exact `kubectl` command to update this Deployment's image to a new version, and separately, the command to roll that back if it caused problems.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `kubectl set image deployment/<name> <container>=<new-image>` to update, and `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>` to roll back — two distinct commands for two distinct situations.

handsOnSteps.instruction: If you have a real cluster, apply your Deployment, then manually delete one of its pods with `kubectl delete pod <one-pod-name>`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: A new pod appears almost immediately (check `kubectl get pods`) to restore the declared 3 replicas — the ReplicaSet noticed the count dropped and fixed it, confirming manually deleting a managed pod doesn't actually 'fix' anything, it just gets replaced.

topics.title: Services and networking within a cluster
topics.concept: Pods are ephemeral -- they get recreated with new internal IP addresses constantly as a Deployment scales or replaces them, so nothing should ever hardcode a pod's IP directly. A SERVICE provides a STABLE network endpoint (a fixed name and virtual IP) that automatically load-balances traffic across whichever pods currently match its label SELECTOR, regardless of how many times those specific pods get replaced underneath. The main Service types: `ClusterIP` (the default -- reachable only from within the cluster, for internal service-to-service communication), `NodePort` (exposes the service on a static port on every node, a simple but limited way to reach it from outside), and `LoadBalancer` (provisions an actual external cloud load balancer, the standard way to expose a service to the public internet on a cloud provider).
topics.analogy: A Service is a company's single published support phone number that always reaches WHOEVER is currently staffing the support desk -- individual staff (pods) rotate in and out constantly, and their personal extensions (pod IPs) change with every rotation, but the one published number (the Service) never changes and always routes to whoever's currently on duty.

examples.code:
# service.yaml -- routes traffic to any pod labeled app: api
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 3000
examples.note: Doc-grounded, not executed against a real cluster in this authoring environment (kubectl is installed here but has no configured cluster context to connect to, and Docker Desktop's own Kubernetes was not enabled) -- this exact YAML/command syntax is verified against Kubernetes' own official documentation. Running it yourself against a real cluster (even a local one like minikube or kind) is the real, required verification step. This exact structure (selector matching a Deployment's pod labels, port = the Service's own port, targetPort = the container's actual listening port) matches the Kubernetes Service API's own official documentation. Any other pod in the cluster can now reach this service simply via the hostname `api-service`, regardless of which specific pods are currently backing it.

mistakes: Hardcoding a specific pod's IP address anywhere in application config -- pod IPs are not stable and change every time a pod is replaced; always use the Service's stable name/endpoint instead.

Using `NodePort` for real public-facing production traffic on a cloud provider -- it's a simple, limited mechanism (accessible via any node's IP on a specific port); `LoadBalancer` is the standard, more robust choice for genuinely public-facing services on cloud infrastructure.

Forgetting a Service's `selector` must match the target pods' actual labels exactly -- a typo or mismatch here silently results in a Service with zero backing pods, and requests to it will simply fail to find anywhere to go.
topics.handsOn: Write a Service manifest of type ClusterIP that routes to pods with a label you choose, matching a Deployment's pod template labels from the previous lesson. Explain which Service type you'd choose instead if this needed to be reachable from the public internet on a cloud provider.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain why Services exist (pod IPs aren't stable), write a Service manifest, and distinguish ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer.

checks.q: Why shouldn't application config ever hardcode a specific pod's IP address to reach another service in the cluster?
checks.a: Pod IPs are not stable -- pods are ephemeral and get replaced constantly (crashes, rolling updates, scaling), each time getting a new IP. A Service provides a stable name/endpoint that automatically routes to whichever pods currently match its selector, regardless of how many times the underlying pods have changed.

keyTakeaways: A Service provides a stable network endpoint that load-balances across pods matching its label selector, since pod IPs aren't stable.
ClusterIP (default, internal-only), NodePort (simple external access via node ports), and LoadBalancer (provisions a real external cloud load balancer) are the main Service types.
A Service's selector must exactly match its target pods' labels, or the Service will have no backing pods to route to.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write a `service.yaml`: `type: ClusterIP`, a `selector` matching a label (e.g. `app: api`) from a Deployment's pod template, and `port`/`targetPort`.
Write one sentence: which Service `type` would you use instead if this needed to be reachable from the public internet on a cloud provider, and why not `NodePort`?
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `LoadBalancer` — it's the standard, robust choice for real public-facing traffic on cloud infrastructure. `NodePort` is simple but limited (accessible only via a specific port on any node's own IP), not meant as the production-grade public entry point.

handsOnSteps.instruction: If you have a real cluster, apply both a Deployment and this matching Service, then run `kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -qO- http://<service-name>`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: A real response body from your app — confirming another pod reached your Deployment's pods purely by the Service's stable name, with zero knowledge of any individual pod's IP.

topics.title: ConfigMaps and Secrets
topics.concept: Application configuration shouldn't be baked into a container image (the same image should run identically across dev/staging/production, with only config differing). A CONFIGMAP holds non-sensitive configuration data (feature flags, URLs, log levels) as key-value pairs, injectable into a pod as environment variables or mounted files. A SECRET holds sensitive data (passwords, API keys, tokens) using the identical mechanism, but Kubernetes stores Secret values base64-ENCODED, not encrypted, by default -- base64 is trivially reversible (the same non-encryption caveat from this path's earlier JWT lesson applies directly here), so a Secret alone is not a real security boundary without additional measures (like encryption-at-rest for the cluster's underlying data store, or an external secrets manager integration) -- Secrets are better understood as a convention that separates sensitive config so it CAN be handled differently (tighter RBAC access, separate rotation), not as automatic encryption.
topics.analogy: A ConfigMap is a shared bulletin board anyone in the building can read (public settings). A Secret is a supposedly locked drawer that's actually only using a translucent, easily-see-through cover (base64) rather than a real lock -- it LOOKS separated and protected, and it IS handled with tighter access rules by convention, but treating that translucent cover as genuine encryption is the exact mistake this lesson warns against.

examples.code:
# configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: api-config
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT: "true"

# secret.yaml (values must be base64-encoded when written directly like this)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: api-secret
type: Opaque
data:
  DATABASE_PASSWORD: cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM=   # base64 of "password123" -- NOT encrypted

# Referencing both in a pod:
#   envFrom:
#     - configMapRef:
#         name: api-config
#     - secretRef:
#         name: api-secret
examples.note: Doc-grounded, not executed against a real cluster in this authoring environment (kubectl is installed here but has no configured cluster context to connect to, and Docker Desktop's own Kubernetes was not enabled) -- this exact YAML/command syntax is verified against Kubernetes' own official documentation. Running it yourself against a real cluster (even a local one like minikube or kind) is the real, required verification step. This exact structure (ConfigMap/Secret manifests, envFrom referencing both via configMapRef/secretRef) matches the Kubernetes ConfigMap and Secret API documentation exactly, including the explicit official caveat that Secret data is base64-encoded, not encrypted, by default.

mistakes: Treating a Kubernetes Secret as inherently encrypted just because it's a distinct resource type from ConfigMap -- by default it's only base64-encoded, which anyone with read access to the Secret (or the cluster's underlying data store) can trivially decode.

Committing a Secret manifest with real base64-encoded credentials directly to a Git repository -- base64 is encoding, not encryption; this is exactly as unsafe as committing the plaintext value, just slightly obfuscated to a casual glance.

Baking environment-specific configuration directly into a container image (e.g. hardcoding a production database URL) -- this defeats the entire point of building one image and configuring it differently per environment via ConfigMaps/Secrets.
topics.handsOn: Write a ConfigMap with 2 non-sensitive settings and a Secret with one sensitive value (base64-encode a sample string yourself to see how trivially reversible it is). Explain what additional measure would actually be needed to make that Secret's contents genuinely protected at rest.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain the difference between a ConfigMap and Secret, and why base64 encoding in a Secret is not the same as real encryption.

checks.q: Is a value stored in a Kubernetes Secret genuinely encrypted by default?
checks.a: No -- by default, Secret values are only base64-ENCODED, which is trivially reversible by anyone with read access, not encrypted. Secrets are a convention that separates sensitive config so it can be handled with tighter access controls, not an automatic encryption mechanism -- real protection at rest requires additional measures like cluster-level encryption-at-rest or an external secrets manager.

keyTakeaways: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive config; Secrets hold sensitive data, both injectable as env vars or mounted files -- keeping config out of the container image itself.
Secret values are base64-encoded by default, not encrypted -- this is trivially reversible, not a real security boundary on its own.
Genuine protection of sensitive values needs additional measures (encryption-at-rest, external secrets managers), not just using the Secret resource type.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write a `configmap.yaml` with 2 plain settings (e.g. `LOG_LEVEL: "info"`).
Base64-encode a sample string yourself: run `echo -n "password123" | base64`.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM=` — and critically, run `echo cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM= | base64 -d` right after to decode it back instantly.
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If decoding it back instantly feels almost too easy, that's the entire point of this step — Secret data being 'base64-encoded' provides zero real confidentiality on its own, only obfuscation from a casual glance.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write a `secret.yaml` using that encoded value under `data:`, `type: Opaque`.
Write one sentence: what ADDITIONAL measure (beyond just using a Secret resource) would actually be needed to protect this value at rest?
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Something like enabling encryption-at-rest for Secrets in the cluster's underlying data store (etcd), and/or using an external secrets manager (Vault, cloud KMS-backed secrets) — a bare Kubernetes Secret alone is not encrypted by default, only encoded.

topics.title: Scaling and self-healing
topics.concept: Scaling a Deployment MANUALLY is a single command (`kubectl scale deployment/name --replicas=5`), but production systems more often use a HORIZONTAL POD AUTOSCALER (HPA), which automatically adjusts a Deployment's replica count based on observed metrics (commonly CPU or memory utilization, or custom metrics) between a configured minimum and maximum -- scaling up under load and back down once demand drops, without a human watching a dashboard and manually adjusting. SELF-HEALING is a related but distinct property: independent of scaling, if any pod fails a configured LIVENESS PROBE (a periodic health check Kubernetes runs against each pod), Kubernetes automatically restarts that specific container -- and if a pod fails a READINESS PROBE, Kubernetes stops routing traffic to it (via the Service) WITHOUT restarting it, since "not ready yet" (e.g. still warming up) is a different condition from "actually broken."
topics.analogy: Autoscaling is a store automatically calling in more staff as the checkout line grows and releasing them once it's quiet, without a manager having to notice and phone people manually. Liveness and readiness probes are two different questions a manager might ask a staff member: liveness asks "are you actually able to work at all" (fails this = replace them), while readiness asks "are you ready for a customer RIGHT NOW" (fails this = just don't send anyone their way for a moment, no need to replace them).

examples.code:
# Adding probes to a Deployment's pod template (excerpt):
#   containers:
#     - name: api
#       image: myregistry.example.com/team/myapp:1.0
#       livenessProbe:
#         httpGet:
#           path: /healthz
#           port: 3000
#         initialDelaySeconds: 10
#         periodSeconds: 15
#       readinessProbe:
#         httpGet:
#           path: /ready
#           port: 3000
#         periodSeconds: 5

# Manual scaling:
# kubectl scale deployment/api-deployment --replicas=5

# Autoscaling (HPA), targeting 60% average CPU utilization, between 2 and 10 replicas:
# kubectl autoscale deployment/api-deployment --cpu-percent=60 --min=2 --max=10

Relying purely on manual `kubectl scale` for a workload with real, variable traffic patterns -- this requires a human to notice load changes and react, exactly the manual toil an HPA exists to eliminate.

checks.q: A pod fails its readiness probe but not its liveness probe. What does Kubernetes do, and why doesn't it restart the container?
checks.a: Kubernetes stops routing traffic to that pod via its Service, but does NOT restart the container. A failed readiness probe means "not ready for traffic right now" (e.g. still warming up or temporarily overloaded), which is different from "broken" (a liveness probe failure) -- restarting a pod that's merely not-yet-ready would be the wrong response.

keyTakeaways: Manual scaling is one kubectl command; a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler automatically adjusts replica count based on observed metrics between a min/max.
A failed liveness probe triggers a container restart -- Kubernetes' self-healing mechanism for genuinely broken pods.
A failed readiness probe only removes a pod from Service traffic routing, without restarting it -- for pods that are temporarily not ready, not broken.

topics.title: Ingress: exposing apps to the outside world
topics.concept: A `LoadBalancer` Service (from the earlier Services lesson) provisions a separate external cloud load balancer PER service -- fine for one or two services, but expensive and unwieldy once you have many services that all need to be reachable from outside. An INGRESS is a single entry point that routes external HTTP(S) traffic to different internal Services based on the request's HOSTNAME or PATH (e.g. `api.example.com` -> the api Service, `example.com/admin` -> the admin Service) -- one shared external load balancer handling routing for many services, instead of one per service. An Ingress resource on its own does nothing; it requires an INGRESS CONTROLLER (like nginx-ingress or a cloud provider's own controller) actually running in the cluster to read Ingress resources and configure real routing accordingly -- a common beginner confusion is creating an Ingress manifest and expecting it to work with no controller installed at all.
topics.analogy: Individual LoadBalancer Services are each service getting its own separate street entrance and doorman -- functional, but expensive and repetitive at scale. An Ingress is one shared main lobby with a single receptionist (the Ingress controller) who reads a directory (the Ingress rules) and directs each visitor to the correct internal office based on which company name or floor they asked for -- one shared entrance serving many internal destinations.

examples.code:
# ingress.yaml -- routes by hostname to different backend Services
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: main-ingress
spec:
  rules:
    - host: api.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api-service
                port:
                  number: 80
    - host: example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /admin
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: admin-service
                port:
                  number: 80

Running it yourself against a real cluster (even a local one like minikube or kind) is the real, required verification step. This exact structure (rules keyed by host, each with paths routing to a backend service by name+port) matches the Kubernetes Ingress API's own official documentation. This manifest alone accomplishes nothing without an Ingress controller (e.g. ingress-nginx) already running in the cluster to actually implement the routing it describes.

mistakes: Creating an Ingress resource and expecting external traffic to start routing correctly with no Ingress controller installed in the cluster -- the Ingress resource is just a declaration; a controller must be running to act on it.

Using a separate LoadBalancer Service per application at real scale -- this provisions (and pays for) a separate external cloud load balancer for every single service, when one Ingress with one shared load balancer can route to all of them.

Forgetting `pathType` (Prefix vs Exact) changes matching behavior meaningfully -- a Prefix match on `/` catches everything under that host, which can unintentionally shadow more specific rules if ordering/specificity isn't considered carefully.

checks.q: You've written a valid Ingress manifest, but external traffic still isn't being routed as described. What's the most likely missing piece?
checks.a: No Ingress controller is running in the cluster. An Ingress resource only describes desired routing rules -- an Ingress controller (like ingress-nginx or a cloud provider's own controller) must actually be installed and running to read those rules and implement real traffic routing.

keyTakeaways: Ingress provides one shared entry point routing external HTTP(S) traffic to many internal Services by hostname/path, instead of a separate LoadBalancer per service.
An Ingress resource alone does nothing -- an Ingress controller must be running in the cluster to actually implement the routing it describes.
Routing rules match on host and path, with pathType affecting exactly how path matching behaves.

topics.title: kubectl and writing YAML manifests
topics.concept: `kubectl` is the primary CLI for interacting with a Kubernetes cluster. Key commands: `kubectl get pods/deployments/services` lists resources (add `-o wide` for more detail); `kubectl describe pod name` shows detailed status/events for one resource -- the first place to look when something's wrong; `kubectl logs pod-name` shows a pod's container output (add `-f` to follow/stream, like `tail -f`); `kubectl apply -f file.yaml` creates or updates resources to match a manifest file DECLARATIVELY (the standard way to manage resources -- re-running `apply` with an updated file just reconciles the difference, rather than needing separate create/update commands); `kubectl delete -f file.yaml` removes whatever that manifest describes. Manifests are written in YAML, which is WHITESPACE-SENSITIVE (indentation defines structure, and unlike some languages, tabs are not accepted -- only spaces) -- a very common real beginner error is an inconsistent-indentation YAML file that fails to parse with a confusing error.
topics.analogy: kubectl is the single remote control for the entire cluster: `get`/`describe`/`logs` are different ways of checking the current state of things (what's on, what's wrong, what's being said), while `apply` is handing over an updated instruction sheet and letting the system figure out exactly what needs to change to match it, rather than you manually specifying every individual adjustment yourself.

examples.code:
kubectl get pods
kubectl get deployments -o wide
kubectl describe pod api-deployment-abc123
kubectl logs api-deployment-abc123 -f
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f service.yaml
kubectl delete -f deployment.yaml
examples.note: Doc-grounded, not executed against a real cluster in this authoring environment (kubectl is installed here but has no configured cluster context to connect to, and Docker Desktop's own Kubernetes was not enabled) -- this exact YAML/command syntax is verified against Kubernetes' own official documentation. Running it yourself against a real cluster (even a local one like minikube or kind) is the real, required verification step. This exact command set and its documented behavior (get for listing, describe for detailed single-resource status/events, logs for container output, apply for declarative create-or-update, delete for removal) matches the official kubectl command reference exactly.

mistakes: Using a mix of tabs and spaces (or inconsistent indentation depth) in a YAML manifest -- YAML is whitespace-sensitive and does not accept tabs at all; this is one of the single most common real beginner errors, producing a parse error that can look confusing at first.

Jumping straight to `kubectl logs` when something's wrong, skipping `kubectl describe` -- describe often reveals the REAL problem faster (a pod stuck in `Pending` due to insufficient cluster resources, or `ImagePullBackOff` because the image name is wrong) that logs alone (which only show output from a container that's actually running) wouldn't reveal.

Manually running `kubectl create` then later `kubectl edit` to make changes, instead of using `kubectl apply -f` consistently -- mixing imperative and declarative approaches on the same resources can cause Kubernetes to lose track of what was declared where, making state harder to reason about over time.
topics.handsOn: List the kubectl commands you'd run, in order, to diagnose why a specific pod isn't starting correctly (assume you don't yet know what's wrong). Then write out what `kubectl apply -f` does differently from a separate create-then-update workflow.
topics.doneWhen: You can name and use the core kubectl commands (get/describe/logs/apply/delete) and explain why kubectl apply is the standard declarative approach to managing resources.

checks.q: A pod is stuck and never starts. Which kubectl command should you check FIRST to understand why, and why not just check the logs?
checks.a: kubectl describe pod name. Logs only show output from a container that's actually running -- a pod stuck in Pending (e.g. insufficient cluster resources) or ImagePullBackOff (e.g. wrong image name) never gets to the point of producing log output at all. describe shows detailed status and recent EVENTS that reveal the real underlying problem.

keyTakeaways: kubectl get/describe/logs inspect cluster state; kubectl apply -f declaratively creates or updates resources to match a manifest file.
kubectl describe is often the fastest way to diagnose a stuck/failing resource -- it shows status and events that logs alone can't.
YAML manifests are whitespace-sensitive (spaces only, no tabs) -- inconsistent indentation is one of the most common real beginner errors.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Without running anything yet, write down the ORDER of kubectl commands you'd run to diagnose a pod that isn't starting: which command first, second, third?
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `kubectl get pods` (spot the problem pod and its STATUS) → `kubectl describe pod <name>` (read the Events section for the real reason) → `kubectl logs <name>` (only useful once the container has actually started running).
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If you jumped straight to `kubectl logs` first, that's a common real ordering mistake — logs only show output from a container that's ACTUALLY running; a pod stuck in `Pending` or `ImagePullBackOff` has no logs yet, and `describe` reveals that faster.

handsOnSteps.instruction: If you have a real cluster, deliberately apply a manifest with a typo'd image name (e.g. `image: nginx:doesnotexist123`), then run your diagnostic order from step 1.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `get pods` shows `ImagePullBackOff` or `ErrImagePull`; `describe pod` explicitly names the failed image pull in its Events — confirming describe surfaces the real cause directly, exactly as this lesson claims.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write one sentence: what does `kubectl apply -f` do differently from a separate create-then-update workflow?
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: `apply` is declarative and idempotent — it creates the resource if it doesn't exist, or updates it to match the file if it does, using the SAME command either way; you don't need to track whether something already exists to know which command to run.

topics.title: Helm: packaging Kubernetes applications
topics.concept: A real application often needs many related manifests (Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Ingress) that must be kept consistent together, and deploying the "same" app to dev/staging/production usually means the same structure with different specific values (replica counts, image tags, resource limits). HELM is the standard PACKAGE MANAGER for Kubernetes: a CHART is a bundle of TEMPLATED manifests plus a `values.yaml` file supplying the specific values that fill in those templates -- `helm install my-release ./mychart --values production-values.yaml` deploys the whole bundle with production-specific values substituted in, and `helm upgrade`/`helm rollback` manage updates and reversions to an entire chart's worth of resources as one coordinated RELEASE, rather than tracking each individual manifest file's state separately by hand.
topics.analogy: Writing raw Kubernetes manifests for a complex app is hand-building furniture from scratch every single time you need a slightly different size. Helm is a well-designed flat-pack furniture kit with clear assembly instructions (the chart's templates) and a single settings sheet (values.yaml) you fill in once per room (per environment) -- same underlying design, consistently assembled, with only the specific measurements changing per use.

examples.code:
# Conceptual Helm chart structure (a real chart has many more files than shown):
# mychart/
#   Chart.yaml           -- chart metadata (name, version)
#   values.yaml          -- default configurable values
#   templates/
#     deployment.yaml     -- a Deployment manifest with {{ .Values.replicaCount }} etc.
#     service.yaml
#     ingress.yaml

# Installing with environment-specific values:
# helm install my-app ./mychart --values production-values.yaml
# Upgrading to a new version/config:
# helm upgrade my-app ./mychart --values production-values.yaml
# Rolling back the whole release if something goes wrong:
# helm rollback my-app 1
examples.note: Doc-grounded, not executed against a real cluster in this authoring environment (kubectl is installed here but has no configured cluster context to connect to, and Docker Desktop's own Kubernetes was not enabled) -- this exact YAML/command syntax is verified against Kubernetes' own official documentation. Running it yourself against a real cluster (even a local one like minikube or kind) is the real, required verification step. This exact chart structure (Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates/ directory with Go-template placeholders like {{ .Values.replicaCount }}) and the install/upgrade/rollback command set matches Helm's own official documentation exactly.

mistakes: Hardcoding environment-specific values directly inside chart templates instead of parameterizing them via values.yaml -- this defeats the entire point of Helm, which is one consistent template set reused across environments via different value files.

Manually editing individual manifests that were deployed via Helm, outside of Helm itself -- this causes drift between what Helm's release history thinks is deployed and what's actually running, similar to the GitOps out-of-band-change problem from the Git module.

Treating Helm as required for every Kubernetes deployment -- for a small number of straightforward, rarely-changing manifests, plain `kubectl apply -f` is simpler and perfectly sufficient; Helm earns its complexity once you have genuinely complex, multi-environment, frequently-updated applications.

checks.q: Why does Helm separate a chart's templates from its values.yaml file instead of hardcoding specific values directly into the manifests?
checks.a: Separating templates from values lets the exact same chart be deployed consistently across different environments (dev/staging/production) by supplying a different values file for each, rather than maintaining separate, drifting copies of the manifests themselves for every environment.

keyTakeaways: Helm is Kubernetes' standard package manager -- a chart bundles templated manifests with a values.yaml supplying the specific values to fill them in.
helm install/upgrade/rollback manage an entire multi-resource application as one coordinated release, not individual manifest files tracked by hand.
Helm earns its complexity for genuinely complex, multi-environment applications -- plain kubectl apply -f remains simpler and sufficient for small, straightforward deployments.

handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: It creates drift between what Helm's own release history believes is deployed and what's actually running in the cluster — the same class of problem as the GitOps out-of-band-change issue from the Git module, just inside Helm's tracking instead of Git's.

title: Infrastructure as Code, Cloud Providers & Observability
why: This final module ties the whole path together: describing infrastructure as code instead of manual clicks, understanding the cloud building blocks (compute/storage/IAM) everything else in this path ultimately runs on, seeing your systems' actual health via monitoring/logging, and a capstone that has you deploy a real containerized app through a CI/CD pipeline -- using the Docker, CI/CD, and Kubernetes skills from every module before this one.

topics.title: Infrastructure as Code and Terraform basics
topics.concept: INFRASTRUCTURE AS CODE (IaC) means defining infrastructure (servers, networks, databases) in version-controlled configuration files rather than manually clicking through a cloud console -- giving infrastructure changes the exact same review/audit/rollback benefits as application code (directly extending this path's earlier GitOps lesson to the infrastructure layer itself, not just application deployments). Terraform is the most widely-used IaC tool, using its own configuration language (HCL) to describe RESOURCES you want to exist; `terraform plan` shows exactly what would change WITHOUT applying anything (a dry run comparing your configuration against Terraform's recorded STATE of what currently exists); `terraform apply` actually creates/updates/destroys resources to match. Terraform tracks a STATE FILE recording what it believes currently exists -- if real infrastructure drifts from that recorded state (e.g. someone manually changed something in the cloud console), Terraform's next plan/apply will detect and attempt to reconcile the difference, the same drift-correction concept as GitOps.
topics.analogy: Manually clicking through a cloud console to create infrastructure is like verbally telling a contractor what to build with no written plan -- there's no record of what was actually decided, and reproducing it exactly (in another environment, or after a mistake) relies entirely on memory. Terraform is a detailed, versioned blueprint: `terraform plan` is the contractor reading it back to you ("here's exactly what I'm about to change") before touching anything, and the recorded state file is a running as-built record of what's actually been constructed so far.

examples.note: Doc-grounded, not executed in this authoring environment (no Terraform installation or real cloud account available here) -- this exact syntax matches the referenced tool's own official documentation. This exact HCL structure (terraform block, provider block, resource block with a TYPE and a local NAME) and the init/plan/apply workflow matches Terraform's own official documentation and its AWS provider's documentation exactly.

mistakes: Manually changing infrastructure in the cloud console that's supposed to be Terraform-managed -- the next `terraform plan` will detect the drift and may propose reverting your manual change back to match the recorded configuration, similar to GitOps reverting an out-of-band Kubernetes change.

Losing or not properly sharing the Terraform state file among a team -- state should be stored remotely (e.g. in a cloud storage backend with locking), not just on one person's laptop, or two people running `apply` simultaneously can corrupt shared infrastructure.

Running `terraform apply` directly without first reviewing `terraform plan`'s output -- plan exists specifically to catch an unintended change (e.g. accidentally destroying a resource) before it actually happens, not after.

checks.q: Why does Terraform's `plan` command exist as a separate step before `apply`, rather than just applying changes directly?
checks.a: `plan` shows exactly what would be created, changed, or destroyed as a dry run, without making any real changes -- letting you review and catch an unintended or dangerous change (like an accidental resource deletion) before it actually happens, rather than discovering it after the fact.

keyTakeaways: Infrastructure as Code defines infrastructure in version-controlled config files, giving it the same review/audit/rollback benefits as application code.
Terraform's plan shows a dry-run diff against its recorded state; apply actually makes the real changes.
Terraform's state file records what it believes currently exists -- drift from manual out-of-band changes is detected and can be reconciled, similar to GitOps.

topics.title: Cloud provider fundamentals: compute, storage, and IAM
topics.concept: Across AWS/Azure/GCP, the same core building blocks recur under different names. COMPUTE runs your actual code: a VIRTUAL MACHINE (AWS EC2, Azure VM, GCP Compute Engine) is a full general-purpose server you manage yourself; a MANAGED CONTAINER SERVICE (AWS ECS/Fargate, Azure Container Apps, GCP Cloud Run) runs containers (built in this path's Docker module) without you managing the underlying servers; SERVERLESS/FUNCTIONS (AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, GCP Cloud Functions) run individual pieces of code in response to events, with no server concept at all from your side. STORAGE splits into OBJECT storage (AWS S3, Azure Blob, GCP Cloud Storage -- for files/blobs, accessed via an API, not a traditional filesystem) and BLOCK storage (a virtual hard disk attached to one VM). IAM (Identity and Access Management) controls exactly who/what can do exactly which actions on which resources -- the PRINCIPLE OF LEAST PRIVILEGE (already introduced for firewalls/security groups) applies directly here: an application's IAM role should be granted only the specific permissions it actually needs, never broad administrator access as a shortcut.
topics.analogy: Choosing a compute option is choosing how much of the building you manage yourself: a VM is renting an entire unfurnished office suite (you handle everything inside it); a managed container service is a serviced office (the building maintains climate/utilities, you just move your desk and equipment in); serverless is paying per meeting-room-hour with zero ongoing commitment at all. IAM is the building's own key-card system: least privilege means every card opens only the specific doors that person's job actually requires, not a master key handed out by default because it's easier to set up that way.

examples.code:
# Conceptual comparison across providers (not executed here -- no live cloud account):
# Task: run a containerized web app, without managing servers directly
#   AWS:   ECS on Fargate, or App Runner
#   Azure: Container Apps, or Azure Container Instances
#   GCP:   Cloud Run
# Task: store user-uploaded files
#   AWS:   S3
#   Azure: Blob Storage
#   GCP:   Cloud Storage
# Task: give a deployed app permission to read from ONE specific storage bucket, nothing else
#   -> an IAM role/policy scoped to exactly that bucket and exactly the read action,
#      not a broad "admin" or "full access" policy applied as a shortcut
examples.note: Conceptual illustration mapping the same core cloud concepts across providers, grounded in each provider's own official service documentation (AWS, Azure, and GCP each publish these exact service names and categorizations).

mistakes: Defaulting to a full VM for a workload that a managed container service or serverless function would handle with far less operational overhead -- reach for the option that manages the LEAST amount of infrastructure you don't actually need to control directly.

Granting an application broad admin/full-access IAM permissions "to avoid permission errors while getting something working" -- this is the exact same shortcut-becomes-permanent risk already seen with security groups: scope permissions to exactly what's needed, and expand deliberately only when a specific new need arises.

Confusing object storage (S3-style, API-accessed blobs) with traditional block storage (a virtual disk attached to a VM, accessed like a normal filesystem) -- they solve different problems and aren't interchangeable; object storage isn't a place to install and run an operating system from.

checks.q: Why is granting an application's IAM role broad "full access" permissions, just to avoid permission errors during setup, a real long-term risk?
checks.a: It violates least privilege -- if that application (or a compromised dependency within it) is ever exploited, it now has far more access than it legitimately needs, dramatically increasing the potential damage. The correct approach is scoping permissions to exactly what's needed and expanding deliberately only when a genuine new need arises, the same principle already established for security groups.

keyTakeaways: Compute options span a spectrum of how much infrastructure you manage: VMs (full control), managed container services (no server management), serverless (no server concept at all).
Storage splits into object storage (API-accessed blobs, like S3) and block storage (a virtual disk attached to one VM) -- different tools for different problems.
IAM's principle of least privilege applies to cloud resources exactly as it does to security groups: grant only what's actually needed, never broad access as a shortcut.
